statement: Runtime check (CapChecker): every accelerator DMA request is looked up by (task ID, pointer ID) in a 256-entry capability table, the compressed 128-bit capability is decoded, and the request is granted only if the capability is tagged, the requested address lies within its bounds, and it holds the permission for the requested read/write; otherwise an exception is raised, a global flag informs the CPU, and the entry's exception bit is set

statement: Tag protection: writes from accelerators always clear the memory tag at the written location, so an accelerator cannot mutate a valid capability into a forged one; tags stay in CPU-owned memory; accelerator DMA carries no capabilities

statement: Non-bypass: only memory requests granted by the CapChecker are forwarded to the memory subsystem; all accelerator memory accesses must pass through it

statement: Unforgeability: capabilities loaded into the CapChecker over the MMIO capability interconnect are preserved inside it, cannot be accessed by the accelerator, are read-only for accelerators, and are managed by a single CPU core

statement: Capability model: accelerator tasks hold capabilities derived from the instantiating CPU task; a leaf's accessible region is a subset of its parent's; buffers used by an accelerator task are allocated by the CPU task and lie within the accelerator task's capability (monotone derivation preserved across the heterogeneous system, c_p = c_a)

assumptions: limitations section
map_note: none

statement: Provenance validity: valid (tagged) capabilities can be constructed only by deriving them from existing valid capabilities; in almost all cases from a single capability (narrowing bounds or permissions), and in a few cases (seal, unseal) from two.  Collectively, unforgeability and guarded manipulation ensure that every dereferenceable capability has valid provenance; all other capabilities are untagged and cannot be dereferenced.
assumptions: From reset state with well-formed roots; tagged memory present; DMA and untagged memory strip tags
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 §2.3.1 L1396-1398; §3.3 L1919; proofs cited at §1.8 L1165 [114] (CHERI-MIPS) and L1173 [11] (Morello)
map_note: RP4: tags cannot be forged because the only tag-setting paths are derivation from a tagged source; RP1: provenance is the inductive hypothesis of reachable-monotonicity

statement: Capability monotonicity: new capabilities must be derived from existing capabilities only via valid manipulations that may narrow (but never broaden) the rights ascribed to the original.  This prevents broadening bounds, increasing permissions, and similar manipulation attacks.
assumptions: Excludes the two deliberate non-monotonic paths (sealed invocation, exception delivery)
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 §2.3.4 L1434; per-instruction monotonicity proofs claimed §12.7 item 4 L10359; [114], [11]
map_note: RP1 (sentry-free, trap-free sequences do not increase authority); RP2 (bounds); RP3 (permissions)

statement: Monotonicity is enforced by four mechanisms: (1) limited expressivity (e.g., permissions modified only by bitwise AND); (2) stripping the tag in register write-back when an instruction attempts a non-monotonic result; (3) exceptions on monotonicity violation (generally avoided); (4) stripping the tag on any data store that overlaps an in-memory capability.  Together these implement non-bypassable capability monotonicity.
assumptions: Choice of mechanism is per-instruction and per-architecture; CHERI ISA v9 uses tag-clearing (ccsr.tc=1)
map_note: RP1: the enumerated mechanisms are the case split a monotonicity proof over the Sail model must discharge; RP4: mechanism (4) is the data-write-clears-tag clause

statement: The two notable exceptions to strict monotonicity are invocation of sealed capabilities (CInvoke, sentry jumps) and exception delivery.  Where non-monotonicity is present, control is transferred to code trusted to use the gain in rights appropriately.
assumptions: Trusted handler/invokee code is outside the ISA guarantee
map_note: RP1: this is exactly the 'sentry-free, trap-free' side condition; G-CF: the firmware is the trusted code that receives the non-monotonic gain

statement: Reachable-rights bound: the rights reachable by executing code are limited to the rights in any capability registers and, inductively, the rights reachable from those capabilities (via loads) but no other rights, which would require a violation of monotonicity.  Delegated rights cannot be used to reach undelegated memory.
assumptions: No sealed-invocation or trap in the sequence; tags in memory intact
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 §2.3.4 L1448; compartment monotonicity named §12.7 item 4 L10359; proved as 'reachable capability monotonicity' for Morello [11] L1173
map_note: RP1: this is the theorem statement (reachable capability monotonicity); G-CF: isolation of a compartment reduces to the closure of its initial register file

statement: Every location that can hold a capability (register or capability-sized, capability-aligned word of memory) has a 1-bit tag that consistently and atomically tracks capability validity.  Register tags are set or cleared only as permitted by guarded manipulation.  Memory tags are not directly addressable via data loads or stores; the capability's addressable fields are protected by the unaddressable tag.
assumptions: Tag granularity is 64-bit or 128-bit per ISA variant
map_note: RP4: tag is out-of-band and unforgeable by data paths; G-c5: tag storage must realise 'not addressable by data loads/stores'

statement: Tags atomically follow capabilities into and out of registers when loaded from or stored to tagged memory.  Stores of non-capability types (bytes, halfwords, words, doublewords, floats) across one or more capability-aligned locations automatically and atomically clear the corresponding tag bits.  Loads without suitable permission clear the register tag.
assumptions: Stores via capability with PERMIT_STORE_CAPABILITY; otherwise tag not stored
map_note: RP4: 'data writes clear tags' verbatim; G-c5: memory subsystem invariant

statement: If untagged memory exists in the system, tags of capability values stored to those locations are discarded, and all capability values loaded from them have the tag unset.
assumptions: Applies to any non-tag-bearing medium (device memory, untagged DRAM, swap)
map_note: G-c5: the NPU SRAM, if untagged, is a tag sink; RP4 holds trivially there

statement: Operations that dereference or otherwise use a capability (load, store, instruction fetch including implicit DDC dereference, seal, unseal, jump, set CID, CInvoke) require the capability to have its tag set; attempting such an operation on an untagged capability causes a precise exception.
assumptions: Per-instruction detail in the instruction reference
map_note: RP4: an unforgeable tag is only meaningful because every authority-exercising instruction checks it; A-1: a per-instruction precondition the Sail model must encode

statement: Regardless of the tag, capability register fields can be extracted and, subject to guarded manipulation, modified; addressable portions can be read with data loads; untagged capability values are simply data and may be moved through capability registers (capability-oblivious copy preserving tags of each location).
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1: establishes that capability contents are not confidential, so the model need not hide them; none for RP1-5

statement: Capabilities contain lower and upper bounds; the address may move out of bounds (and back) without faulting, but any dereference (load, store, instruction fetch) via an out-of-bounds capability throws a hardware exception.  Compression restricts how far out of bounds an address may go before the capability becomes unrepresentable.
assumptions: Representable-range limit per CHERI Concentrate
map_note: RP2: bounds are a hard check on every dereference; none widen by address arithmetic

statement: CAndPerm: cd := cs1 with perms := perms AND rs2[hperms bits] and uperms := uperms AND rs2[uperms bits]; if cs1 was sealed, cd.tag is cleared.  Permissions are therefore modified only by bitwise AND and cannot express an increase.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP3: permissions never grow (limited-expressivity mechanism)

statement: The capability flags field may be manipulated freely; it does not determine privilege, and its state is orthogonal to capability monotonicity (it affects semantics of access, e.g. CHERI-RISC-V encoding mode, not access control).
assumptions: None
map_note: none: a monotonicity proof must exclude flags from the order, with a clause that mode-flipping does not by itself change authority

statement: Sealing marks a capability immutable and non-dereferenceable: attempts to modify a sealed capability clear the tag, and attempts to dereference or jump to it (other than via the unsealing invocation paths) raise exceptions.  Two forms exist: object-type-sealed pairs and sealed entry (sentry) capabilities.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP5: sentries are opaque (immutable, non-dereferenceable); RP1: unsealing is the controlled non-monotonic step

statement: CInvoke checks that both operand capabilities are valid, both sealed, the code capability executable, the data capability non-executable, and that their object types match; it then atomically unseals them into PCC and the invoked-data register (C31 in CHERI-RISC-V), with bit 0 of the address cleared.  This is a constrained form of non-monotonicity.
assumptions: PERMIT_INVOKE on both operands (Table 3.1)
map_note: RP1: the only register-file-level non-monotonic instruction; its precondition set is the clause a reachable-monotonicity theorem must carve out

statement: Sealed entry (sentry) capabilities are immutable by their bearer and do not authorise memory loads or stores; the jump instruction atomically unseals the sentry and installs it in PCC.  CSealEntry derives a sentry from any PERMIT_EXECUTE capability, preserving permissions, bounds and cursor (an ambient monotonic action).  Sentries have otype 2^XLEN-2 and are not intended to be unsealable within general system software except by entry of control flow.
assumptions: Footnote 5: the primordial root can unseal otype 2^XLEN-2 unless boot code partitions roots to exclude it
map_note: RP5: sentries are opaque (non-dereferenceable, immutable, enter-only); the footnote is an explicit boot-time assumption for G-CF

statement: CJALR writes the next-instruction PCC to cd sealed as a sentry, and installs cs1 (address + imm, bit 0 cleared) into PCC, unsealing it if it is a sentry.  Exception return (xRET) likewise atomically unseals a sentry when installing it to PCC.  CHERI-RISC-V creates a sentry whenever PCC is stored to a link register.
assumptions: Only sentries are unsealed by jump/xRET; otype-sealed capabilities raise seal violation
map_note: RP5: return addresses are opaque sentries; RP1: a jump through a sentry is the 'sentry' side condition

statement: Capability flow control is provided by three mechanisms: capability PTE bits (load-capability stripping tags on load; store-capability raising an exception), capability load/store permission bits on capabilities, and the GLOBAL/PERMIT_STORE_LOCAL_CAPABILITY colouring (local capabilities may be stored only via a capability with store-local permission).
assumptions: Local/global feature 'remains under development'
map_note: G-CF: these are the primitives the firmware uses to bound capability propagation between tenants

statement: Separate PERMIT_LOAD_CAPABILITY / PERMIT_STORE_CAPABILITY permissions allow two protected subsystems to share a buffer with data load/store but no capability load/store permission; such subsystems cannot pass capabilities via the shared buffer even if they collude.  (Recognised as a requirement when formally modelling CHERI's guarantees.)
assumptions: Both subsystems' only path to the buffer is via such capabilities
map_note: G-CF: the tenant-to-tenant shared-memory channel is data-only by construction

statement: The CHERI Concentrate compression model maintains monotonicity: no ISA manipulation of a capability can grant increased rights, and when unrepresentable cases are generated (pointer substantially out of bounds, very unaligned object) the capability becomes un-dereferenceable (tag cleared).  The fast representability check composes inRange, inLimit and E>=50.
assumptions: 128-bit format with MW=14 (Morello uses different constants); SMT checks of compression properties per §12.7 item 5
map_note: RP2: the encoding itself must not widen bounds on any address update; this is the lemma that bridges in-memory bits to the abstract bounds

statement: CSetBounds: cd := cs1 with base := cs1.address and length := rs2; if not exactly representable, base rounds down and length rounds up by the smallest amount forming a representable capability covering the request; cd.tag is cleared if the result's bounds exceed cs1's bounds or cs1 was sealed.  Bounds on a returned capability are never broader than those of the input, and narrowing is itself monotonic.
assumptions: CSetBoundsExact clears the tag instead when rounding would occur
map_note: RP2: bounds never widen, stated as a per-instruction postcondition over the rounded result

statement: CSetAddr / CIncOffset / CSetOffset: the address is replaced or incremented; if the resulting capability cannot be represented exactly (bounds would decode differently), or cs1 was sealed, cd.tag is cleared; remaining fields are what the in-memory representation decodes to.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP2 and RP4: address arithmetic can only lose the tag, never silently change bounds

statement: Unforgeability is implemented by two means: tag bits and guarded manipulation.  Each capability register and each capability-aligned physical memory location has a tag; directly overwriting a capability in memory with a data store clears the tag; data without a valid tag may be loaded into a register but dereferencing or invoking it traps.  Guarded manipulation: instructions that manipulate capability fields are not able to increase the rights associated with a capability; sealed capabilities can be unsealed only via invocation or the unseal instruction under the same monotonicity rules.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP4 (tags) and RP1/RP3 (guarded manipulation) stated together as the definition of unforgeability

statement: Intentionality: load, store, and jump instructions never automatically select integer versus capability semantics based on the presence of a tag; there are no associative lookups of capabilities; every instruction is clearly defined as expecting an integer or a tagged capability operand and fails if that expectation is not met.
assumptions: DDC is the one implicit (but still single, named) authorising capability
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 §3.2 goal 6 L1885; §3.3 L1921; §3.7 L2540; §4.3.4 L3253
map_note: A-1: the authorising capability of every instruction is a syntactic function of the opcode, which is what makes a per-instruction authority predicate well-defined; G-c: the RTL must not add tag-dependent decode paths

statement: Design goal 12: CHERI uses provable, deterministic protection, avoiding probabilistic techniques and architectural secrets; CHERI's architectural safety properties must be formally expressible, deterministically true, and mechanically provable from that expression.
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1: the specification itself commits to mechanised provability, which is the licence for AIVHAI's Sail-to-Rocq route

statement: Table 3.1 permission semantics: every architectural permission requires a valid tag; PERMIT_EXECUTE/LOAD/STORE require an unsealed capability and an address bounds check; PERMIT_SEAL/UNSEAL require unsealed and an object-type bounds check; PERMIT_INVOKE requires a sealed capability; PERMIT_SET_CID requires a CID bounds check; permissions grant only subject to the current architectural ring and always restrict relative to the existing security model.
assumptions: Per-instruction requirements in the instruction reference
map_note: RP3: the permission lattice and its side conditions; A-1: the table is the check matrix a Sail model must satisfy instruction by instruction

statement: CHERI relies on tagged physical memory: a 1-bit tag with each capability-sized, capability-aligned physical location, so that memory mapped at multiple virtual addresses yields the same tags regardless of the virtual address used.  Tags must be atomically bound to the data they protect and are expected to be cached with that data in the cache hierarchy.
assumptions: Coherent cache hierarchy
map_note: G-c5: tag storage integrity is defined over physical addresses, so the NPU/DMA path must preserve the same physical tag

statement: Strong atomicity: it must not be possible to partially overwrite a capability value in memory while retaining the tag, or to partially load a capability and have the tag set.  Atomicity here concerns visibility of partial or interleaved results (which must not occur for capability stores or tag clearing during data overwrite), not ordering or progress, which follow the host memory model; atomicity is with respect to lines in the local cache, not global state.
assumptions: Host architecture memory model (RVWMO for CHERI-RISC-V) governs ordering
map_note: G-c5: the tag-storage integrity obligation in one sentence; RP4: a torn write must never leave a tagged, corrupted capability

statement: Reset invariants: all capability registers intended as roots are initialised with tag set, offset 0 (PCC: boot vector), base 0, length 2^XLEN, otype 2^XLEN-1, all permission bits set, unused bits cleared; non-root registers are untagged with the NULL-like shape.  At least a root PCC and a root data capability must exist from inception.
assumptions: Concrete architectures specify reset flags; CHERI-RISC-V Table 4.3 gives per-SCR reset to infinity or NULL
map_note: A-1: the initial state of any reachability proof; G-CF: the firmware's authority at boot is exactly these roots

statement: Tags in memory are not guaranteed cleared on CPU reset; firmware or the software supervisor must ensure pages placed into use (especially by untrustworthy code) have been cleared.  DRAM may contain malformed capabilities with the tag set; a CHERI instruction never creates a malformed capability from a well-formed one, and initial register contents are never malformed.
assumptions: Hardware may or may not guard against malformed capabilities; if not, the OS zeroing obligation is load-bearing
map_note: G-CF: page clearing before delegation is a firmware obligation; G-c5: residual tags in DRAM across reset are a tag-storage hazard; A-1: well-formedness is an invariant the model must carry

statement: Instruction fetch is authorised by PCC: the fetch traps if PCC is out of bounds, untagged, sealed (non-sentry), or lacks PERMIT_EXECUTE.  Exceptions are thrown on the jump where possible (for debuggability) and additionally on fetch, to catch exception return to an invalid or out-of-bounds capability.  In CHERI-RISC-V, when a trap/ecall/xRET installs an SCR value into PCC that would not be a valid PCC, the value is still installed and the next fetch raises a further exception.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP1: control flow cannot escape PCC bounds; G-CF: trap-vector capabilities (xTCC) are checked on fetch, not on install

statement: Guarded-manipulation failures (attempted non-monotonic operations, unrepresentable bounds) strip the tag from the written-back capability rather than trapping; the exception is deferred to the attempted dereference.  CHERI-RISC-V reports this via the read-only ccsr.tc bit, which a compliant implementation sets to 1 at reset.  Stripping also avoids encouraging speculation-vulnerable implementations.
assumptions: Checks must still be performed before forwarding the result
map_note: RP1/RP4: the failure mode of every monotonicity violation is a cleared tag, so 'authority never increases' holds even on the failing path

statement: When PERMIT_LOAD_CAPABILITY (or the equivalent page-table permission) is absent, the tag on a loaded capability is stripped rather than raising an exception; [C]LC clears cd.tag if the authorising capability (DDC in integer mode, cs1 in capability mode) lacks PERMIT_LOAD_CAPABILITY.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP4: loads cannot manufacture a tag the authorising capability does not permit; G-CF: tag-stripping copies at compartment boundaries

statement: On exception entry the architecture must save a copy of the full PCC, not just PC; CHERI-RISC-V provides xEPCC, xTCC, xTDC, xScratchC per ring.  It is essential that capability register values are not merely saved/restored but also not leaked: the handler must restore or clear registers so that capabilities used by the handler or another context are not exposed to the interrupted context.
assumptions: Register clearing is a software (TCB) obligation, not a hardware guarantee
map_note: G-CF: the firmware trap path must satisfy the no-leak obligation; RP1: exception delivery is the 'trap' side condition

statement: Capability-triggered exceptions have priority above alignment faults and MMU faults (page-table/TLB misses), because capability processing logically occurs before a virtual address is interpreted; this prevents triggering a page fault on an address outside capability bounds.  CHERI-RISC-V Table 4.5 fixes the order: ACCESS_SYSTEM_REGISTERS > Tag > Seal > Type > INVOKE/SET_CID > EXECUTE > LOAD/STORE > LOAD_CAP/STORE_CAP > STORE_LOCAL_CAP > GLOBAL > Length > Software-defined permission.
assumptions: Other priority rules are 'less security critical' but defined for determinism
map_note: G-c: the RTL exception-priority encoder must refine this order; A-1: the model's exception function must be deterministic in this order

statement: Capabilities are interpreted relative to the current virtual address space (physical when translation is disabled; in M-mode generally physical, honouring mstatus.MPRV for data).  Capability processing yields an allow/reject decision plus a virtual address and length, which then proceeds through the normal MMU path; the capability mechanism therefore never enables an operation not already permitted by MMU checks.
assumptions: Capabilities carry no ASID; the TCB must limit cross-address-space capability flow
map_note: G-CF: isolation is the conjunction of capability bounds and the firmware's address-space configuration; the MMU is a second, independent check

statement: PERMIT_ACCESS_SYSTEM_REGISTERS on PCC is required to configure the MMU (enable/disable translation, set satp, flush TLB), to access SCRs other than PCC/DDC, and to read or write any CSR except the whitelist (cycle, time, instret, hpmcounter read-only; fflags, frm, fcsr read-write).  Absence of the permission denies privileged features; presence does not grant them unless the ring also authorises.
assumptions: Ring-based privilege retained; permission only restricts
map_note: G-CF: in-kernel/firmware compartmentalisation rests on this bit; it is the capability analogue of the SecureState CU0=false condition

statement: CHERI currently does not control memory accesses performed by the page-table walker via physical addresses; constraining the walker with capabilities is future work (Appendix C.13.4).
assumptions: Explicit scope exclusion
map_note: G-CF: a residual assumption that must be written on the firmware isolation proof (walker trusted; page tables protected by PMP/other means)

statement: MMU capability permissions: with the load-capability page permission absent, architectures may trap or clear the loaded tag (CHERI-RISC-V: CR/CRM/CRG select strip, fault, unaltered; reserved encodings fault); with the store-capability permission absent, a store of a tagged capability traps (CHERI-RISC-V: CW=0 traps with code 0x1B; CW=1,CD=0 either faults or atomically sets CD).  The PTW must check V, U, W first, then CW, before atomically asserting D/CD; D/A take precedence over CD.  Implementations must take a data-dependent disposition (fault only when the tag is set).
assumptions: Sv39/Sv48 only; Sv32 acts as if CW, CD, CR set and CRM, CRG clear
map_note: G-CF: per-page capability flow control is the firmware's coarse-grained tenant boundary; G-c: the PTW check ordering is an RTL refinement obligation

statement: A capability dirty bit may substitute for trapping on failed capability store; false positives are permissible as for the page dirty bit, but false negatives (bit not set although a tagged capability was stored via the page) are not permissible, or revocation and garbage collection might miss a capability.
assumptions: Only where dirty-bit tracking is supported
map_note: G-CF: soundness of any firmware revocation sweep depends on this no-false-negative clause

statement: DMA recommendation 1: in the absence of additional support, DMA access to memory must be unable to write tagged values and must implicitly strip tags on the locations it writes, so that only the CPU can introduce capabilities into the system and DMA cannot introduce capabilities without valid provenance or corrupt CPU-originated capabilities.
assumptions: Non-capability-aware DMA engine
map_note: G-c5: the DMA/MMU mediation shim must clear tags on every DMA write (the minimum property); RP4: 'data writes clear tags' extended to non-CPU writers

statement: DMA recommendation 2: capability-aware DMA (able to load and store tagged values) must be the remit only of trustworthy DMA engines that preserve valid provenance, ensure monotonicity, and so on; capabilities must be evaluated with respect to an address space (physical if no IOMMU, else an I/O virtual address space), and care is needed so capabilities are used only where they have meaning.  Capabilities held by devices are hard to locate for revocation.
assumptions: Trustworthiness of the DMA engine is assumed, not proved
map_note: G-c5 and G-CF: a capability-aware Coral NPU is exactly this 'trustworthy DMA engine'; the obligations named (provenance, monotonicity, address-space scoping) are the shim's proof obligations

statement: C.14 scope: distributed capabilities for peripherals assume peripherals are capability-aware (able to load, store and manipulate capabilities and tags); hardware that is not capability-aware and uses integer pointers is out of scope, though it may be constrained or capability-wrapped by some other structure.  Scenarios range from trustworthy hardware and software to untrustworthy hardware and software.
assumptions: Experimental feature; no instruction definitions
map_note: G-c5: AIVHAI's NPU lands in the 'capability-aware peripheral' scope; the integer-pointer case is the fallback shim design

statement: C.14 enforcement: bridges (ATPUs) enforce colours, may disallow capabilities of other colours, and bridges closer to DRAM may disallow capabilities accepted further away; processing elements enforce the remainder of the capability model (monotonicity, tagging) within their local software.  Most conservatively a PE deals only with capabilities of its own colour, treating any other-coloured capability as if its tag were cleared.  An untrustworthy PE may corrupt its own capabilities but, because colouring is enforced by the bridge, harms only its own software.
assumptions: Colour representation reuses otype bits (unspecified); experimental
map_note: G-c5/G-CF: a hierarchy-of-trust argument for a bus-level guard that AIVHAI's DMA/MMU shim can instantiate; the 'untrustworthy PE harms only itself' sentence is the confinement claim

statement: C.14 colour change is a privileged instruction taking an input capability and an authorisation capability; the output is the input with colour changed to match the authorisation; checks may be necessary that the input is a subset of the authorisation capability, bearing in mind the address spaces may lack a contiguous mapping; a PE lacking suitable authority must call out to a more trustworthy component.
assumptions: Implementation outline only
map_note: RP1: cross-address-space translation of a capability must remain a subset operation; G-CF: the firmware would hold the colour-authority capabilities

statement: CHERI-RISC-V register file: when a register is written as an integer, the new value is stored in the bottom XLEN bits and the top XLEN bits and tag are cleared to those of NULL; integer reads use only the bottom XLEN bits.  This prevents in-register corruption of tagged capabilities by implicitly clearing the tag.
assumptions: Unified integer/capability register file
map_note: RP4: integer writes are the register-file analogue of data stores clearing memory tags; CVA6-CHERI's merged register file must refine this (G-c)

statement: Strong type safety for capability-aware instructions: all instructions explicitly encode whether an integer or capability operand is used (or the mode unambiguously specifies it), and attempts to use untagged values where tagged ones are expected lead to an exception.  Memory and control-flow instructions never condition behaviour on the tag.
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1: per-opcode operand typing is a static property of the Sail decode the model must preserve

statement: When CHERI is disabled for a lower privilege level via menvcfg/senvcfg bit 28, CHERI instructions trap as illegal, but bounds and permissions on PCC and DDC are always honoured, exceptions always copy PCC to xEPCC and restore the full PCC on return, and capability mode is honoured if enabled in PCC; software disabling CHERI must set PCC and DDC suitably.
assumptions: Bit allocation may change before ratification
map_note: G-CF: legacy (non-CHERI) tenants remain bounded by PCC/DDC, so the isolation claim does not depend on tenant code being CHERI-aware

statement: Where an SCR extends a RISC-V CSR (MTCC/mtvec, MEPCC/mepc, MScratchC/mscratch, and S/U analogues), a CSR read returns the SCR's address and a CSR write sets the SCR's address exactly as CSetAddr would, so a sealed capability in an SCR cannot be modified tag-preservingly; CSR legalisation (write-ignore bits) applies to the new address; CSpecialRW of a sealed capability into an SCR extending a CSR with non-preserved bits clears the tag even if the address would be unchanged; an unrepresentable result clears the tag but preserves address and metadata.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP5: sentries held in trap-vector SCRs stay opaque under legacy CSR writes; A-1: an aliasing invariant between CSR and SCR state the model must maintain

statement: Capability encoding mode (PCC flag): in integer mode address operands of existing opcodes are integer-relative and DDC's tag must be valid with all capability checks performed; in capability mode they are capability-relative with the operand's tag valid and all checks performed; the interpretation is never ambiguous in either mode.  Mode must be correctly observed on exception entry (xTCC should carry the handler's mode).
assumptions: Legacy loads/stores disabled by installing an untagged DDC
map_note: G-CF: mode is part of the per-compartment context the firmware must save/restore; RP1: mode switching changes decoding, not authority

statement: CBuildCap: cd := cs1 with base, length, address, perms, uperms, flags taken from cs2 (sealed as a sentry if cs2 is one); if the result is not a subset of cs1 in bounds or permissions, or is not legally derivable, or cs1 is untagged or sealed, cd := cs2 with tag cleared.  CBuildCap is intended not to change the set of reachable capabilities (it is rederivation).
assumptions: 'Legally derivable' includes representability
map_note: RP1: the one instruction that sets a tag from untagged bits, and its subset precondition is what keeps reachable authority unchanged

statement: CSeal: cd := cs1 sealed with otype := cs2.address; tag cleared if cs2 cannot authorise sealing (tag, PERMIT_SEAL, bounds over otype space) or cs1 was already sealed.  CUnseal: cd := cs1 unsealed using cs2 as authority; GLOBAL is stripped from cd if cs2 lacks GLOBAL; tag cleared if cs2 cannot authorise.  CCSeal: conditional seal that passes the input through in defined cases and otherwise clears the tag on failure.
assumptions: Sealing authority is itself a capability (PERMIT_SEAL/UNSEAL with otype bounds)
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 §7.4 CSeal L6252, CUnseal L6880, CCSeal L5133; §9.18 L9374
map_note: RP5: unsealing is explicit and authority-gated; RP3: CUnseal can only strip GLOBAL, never add permissions

statement: CTestSubset: rd := 1 iff cs1.tag == cs2.tag and the bounds and permissions of cs2 are a subset of those of cs1.  The microarchitectural bounds-check unit must support the <= comparison and extended-precision top needed by CSetBounds and TestSubset.
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1: an ISA-visible subset predicate that can serve as the executable oracle for RP2/RP3 in model-based testing

statement: CLoadTags returns the tags of a power-of-two number (1..XLEN) of consecutive capabilities at and above cs1.address; the result is coherent with other processors, as if the corresponding data words had been loaded; typical implementations return one L1 line's tags without allocating in the cache.
assumptions: Implementation-defined count
map_note: G-c5: tag reads must be coherent with data; useful as a hardware-level observation point for tag-storage integrity testing

statement: Unpredictable behaviour: for CHERI to be secure, programs whose behaviour is 'unpredictable' per the base ISA must not modify memory or capability registers in a way that bypasses the capability mechanism; the easy way is that unpredictable cases modify neither memory nor capability registers.  The CHERI1 test suite checks the FPGA follows known behaviour in such cases.
assumptions: Stated for CHERI-MIPS; carries over as a modelling obligation for any base ISA with UNSPECIFIED behaviour
map_note: A-1 and G-c: every UNSPECIFIED/implementation-defined point in the RISC-V base must be pinned by the AIVHAI model so the hardware cannot hide an authority increase there

statement: TLB bypass: code able to modify the TLB can bypass the capability mechanism by remapping a protected physical page to a virtual address it holds a capability for.  Mitigations: OS forbids user TLB modification (security then depends on OS correctness); a high-assurance microkernel proof must show untrusted code cannot regain the TLB-modifying state except by re-entering the kernel via syscall or exception; or omit the TLB.
assumptions: MIPS CP0 state names; the RISC-V analogue is satp/MMU control gated by PERMIT_ACCESS_SYSTEM_REGISTERS
map_note: G-CF: the firmware isolation theorem must include 'tenant cannot reach translation-controlling state' as an invariant, exactly as SecureState does

statement: Constants in the formal model: because L3 has no named-constant notion, machine-checked proofs may need to prove that certain 'constants' (e.g., endianness) are in fact constant, since changing them would change the effect of a capability dereference.
assumptions: L3-era remark; Sail has proper constants
map_note: A-1: model-hygiene obligation; configuration registers that alter memory interpretation must be shown immutable from unprivileged state

statement: Reference-monitor security requirement of the hardware: untrusted code runs for a while and eventually returns control to trusted code, and on re-entry (a) it is entered at one of a small number of known entry points, (b) its code, data and stack have not been modified by the untrusted code, and (c) the reserved capability registers have not been modified.  'Cannot be bypassed' and 'tamperproof' mean there is no way within the ISA to modify the reference monitor's reserved memory or registers: all memory accesses are checked against a capability register and succeed only if permitted.
assumptions: No physical access; covert channels excluded; attacker runs arbitrary machine code (compiler not in TCB, §9.4)
map_note: G-CF: this is the shape of AIVHAI's firmware-isolation claim (structural non-bypass, not semantic benignity)

statement: SecureState predicate (conjunction): CP0.Status.KSU != 0, CU0 = false, EXL = false, ERL = false; TLB fully initialised with valid page masks and no (ASID, VA) matching multiple entries; the untrusted address set SU maps to no trusted code/data/stack and to no memory-mapped I/O device (else the proof must show the device cannot DMA outside SU); SU is cached memory; all capability registers and all capabilities within SU have base+length <= 2^64 or tag = false; every non-reserved capability register and every capability in SU is untagged, or sealed with an otype outside TU, or grants neither ACCESS_SYSTEM_REGISTERS, nor access outside SU, nor otype space outside TU; and if in a branch delay slot the same holds of the branch-target PCC.
assumptions: Trusted code establishes SecureState before calling untrusted code
map_note: G-CF: the inductive invariant template for a CF isolation proof; the 'I/O device cannot DMA outside SU' clause is precisely the NPU/DMA obligation AIVHAI must discharge (G-c5)

statement: Reference-monitor theorem outline: SecureState => X(SecureState or TCBEntryState), hence by induction SecureState => TCBEntryState R SecureState (weak until).  Adding CP0.Status.IE = true and IM(7) = true gives SecureStateTimer, and since Count increases by at least one per instruction, SecureStateTimer => F TCBEntryState and SecureStateTimer => SecureStateTimer U TCBEntryState.
assumptions: 'Semi-formal outline' in the document; full proofs of related isolation properties are in [114]
map_note: G-CF: isolation (R) and liveness-of-return (U, via timer) are stated separately, matching AIVHAI's refusal to fold availability into isolation (SL-AIVHAI-P04)

statement: Step lemmas of the reference-monitor argument: with KSU != 0, CU0/EXL/ERL false, every instruction either raises an exception (X TCBEntryState) or leaves CP0 and the TLB unchanged; with the TLB in SecureState, loads/stores are not undefined due to multiple matches; the capability instructions preserve the SecureState clauses about capability registers and SU; stores may trap but cannot modify locations outside SU; without ACCESS_SYSTEM_REGISTERS the reserved registers are not modified; residual 'unpredictable' cases require a CHERI-specific refinement of the base ISA.
assumptions: L3 model conflates MIPS 'undefined' and 'unpredictable'
map_note: RP1: 'capability instructions preserve the SecureState clauses' is per-instruction monotonicity used as a lemma; G-CF: the remaining lemmas are the privilege-state invariants

statement: Confidentiality and the refinement paradox: confidentiality properties are not preserved by refinement; any non-determinism in the ISA specification may be refined into a leak, and an implementation may leak via microarchitectural covert channels (caches).  To reduce Meltdown-class risk, implementations should perform MMU and all capability checks (tag, bounds, permissions, seal) before a load or store rather than speculatively executing it first.
assumptions: Covert channels explicitly out of scope of the ISA argument
map_note: G-c: an ISA-refinement proof gives integrity/non-bypass, not confidentiality; AIVHAI's 'structural non-bypass, not side-channel freedom' scoping is grounded here

statement: PCC bounds in the pipeline: CHERI-MIPS/RISC-V are designed so that no representability check is ever needed on PCC modification, by throwing an out-of-bounds exception on the branch using the general bounds check; all open-source implementations bounds-check PCC for every instruction executed; branch targets are guaranteed in-bounds, so per-instruction checks could be elided or batched.
assumptions: Open-source Piccolo/Flute/Toooba behaviour
map_note: G-c: an RTL-level invariant (PCC always in bounds at fetch) that CVA6-CHERI must refine; RP2 at the control-flow level

statement: CHERI requires atomic memory access to capability-wide words (e.g., 129 bits).  Open-source implementations widen core-to-cache paths to capability width; where memory paths past L1 are half-width, a capability is never split between bursts and the tag is duplicated on both flits (AXI USER field); Morello's 32-byte capability-pair stores are cracked into two micro-ops that must atomically both succeed or both fail.
assumptions: Specific to the named microarchitectures
map_note: G-c5: the bus-level realisation of tag/data atomicity; the AXI tag-sideband convention is directly relevant to the NPU/DMA shim

statement: Data-dependent store faults: the architecture requires that address and data be inspected before a store issues, because PERMIT_STORE_LOCAL_CAPABILITY on the authorising capability may fault depending on the GLOBAL bit of the capability being stored; high-performance designs that separate address and data issue must delay address issue until the stored tag and GLOBAL bit are available.
assumptions: Could be relaxed if STORE_LOCAL is dropped
map_note: G-c: an RTL refinement obligation on the CVA6-CHERI store path

statement: Tagged memory realisation: one extra bit per capability word (129-bit words for CHERI-128); caches may store tags in data banks or aggregated per line; a separate tag cache must solve coherency and ensure tag and data pairs are always accessed atomically; external memory may use a tag controller with a hierarchical in-memory tag table (TagController), ECC spare bits, or a dedicated tag channel.
assumptions: Open-source TagController used in all open-source implementations
map_note: G-c5: the design space for tag storage; every option must satisfy the §3.5.2 atomic-binding invariant (P-B2-028)

statement: Speculative Capability Constraint (SCC): no capability should exist in registers or forwarding paths beyond the capabilities in the latest committed architectural register file, those transitively reachable through them, and less-powerful capabilities derived from these.  Required features: capability-guarded cache access (permissions and bounds verified before any cache access; all open-source implementations do this), PCC bounds forwarding rather than prediction (Toooba violates this), and speculative forgery prevention.
assumptions: Recommendation, not an architectural requirement
map_note: G-c: SCC is the speculative lift of RP1 (reachable monotonicity extended to transient state); defence-in-depth, outside AIVHAI's formal boundary but a stated hardware obligation

statement: Speculative forgery prevention: capability manipulation instructions should not speculatively produce capabilities with privilege greater than their operands; CBuildCap, CSetBounds and CUnseal must not forward tagged results before their checks complete (open-source implementations are believed to forward unsafely; Toooba likely vulnerable); value speculation must never produce a valid capability; tag-clearing architectures (Morello) are expected to be immune.
assumptions: Microarchitectural recommendation
map_note: RP4 at the microarchitectural level: no transient tag may be synthesised; G-c clause for CVA6-CHERI's forwarding network

statement: Formal methodology (chapter 12): (1) PVS semantics of CHERI-MIPS for expressibility, proofs about critical code, and test generation; (2) BSV-to-PVS/SAL export, Smten SMT modelling; (3) L3 then Sail models of CHERI-MIPS as the golden model validated against the test suite and used to find hardware bugs and software reliance on undefined behaviour; (4) L3/Sail exported to HOL4, Isabelle, Coq for mechanised proof of per-instruction monotonicity, compression-scheme properties, and compartment monotonicity (arbitrary code in a compartment cannot construct rights beyond those reachable from the register file or loadable capabilities); (5) SMT problems generated from Sail to check compression; (6) impact on C semantics.
assumptions: Text says the CHERI-MIPS proofs are 'to be documented in future papers'; §1.8 and §10 cite [114] (Oakland 2020) for them and [11] (ESOP 2022) for Morello
map_note: A-1: the Sail model is the golden model and the proof source; the named property set (per-instruction monotonicity, compression, compartment monotonicity) is the RP1-RP3 trio

statement: Threat model: CHERI constrains code in execution; physical attacks are explicitly excluded; electromagnetic and acoustic side channels are not countered; CHERI is an ISA-level model that does not address CPU- or bus-level covert and side-channel attacks and relies on the microarchitecture to limit implicit flows.
assumptions: Scope statement
map_note: none directly; it is the scoping clause AIVHAI inherits (SL-AIVHAI-P04)

statement: Isolation via CHERI: capability nonforgeability, monotonicity and provenance validity ensure that constrained software cannot create new rights and cannot escalate existing rights; isolation is a continuing condition, so discretion in delegating capabilities must be maintained throughout execution, as MMU isolation depends on safe continuing configuration.  Compartmentalisation (beyond isolation) uses the two non-monotonic mechanisms, exception handling and jump-based invocation; it is essential that exercise of non-monotonicity reliably transfers control to code trusted with the new rights.  Zeroing memory before reuse prevents leakage of rights, not just data.
assumptions: Scheduling, resource allocation and fresh-memory non-leakage are higher-level supervisor properties
map_note: G-CF: the firmware's isolation claim decomposes into (i) initial register-file closure, (ii) continuing delegation discipline, (iii) trusted receivers of non-monotonic transfers, (iv) zeroing on reuse

statement: Overwriting capabilities in memory: if a valid in-memory capability is partly overwritten by an untagged data store the tag is cleared, making it an invalid capability; stores need not read the old tag (write, not read-modify-write); a consequence is that capability contents cannot be kept secret from a program that holds them.
assumptions: None
map_note: RP4: 'data writes clear tags' with its rationale; G-c5: the memory subsystem must clear, not merge, on partial overwrite

statement: NULL has the tag unset with base and length fields zero in the abstract model (length reported as MAXINT = 2^64-1 under compression so that every offset is representable); consequently zero-filling a region initialises every capability-sized word to NULL, and all-zero memory contains no authority.
assumptions: Compression constants
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 §9.14 L9322-9330; §9.15 L9334-9338; §3.4.3 'The NULL Capability' L2111
map_note: G-c5/G-CF: page zeroing is sufficient to remove rights, which the firmware's clearing obligation (P-B2-030) relies on

statement: Permission bits plus otype determine the kind of a capability (memory capability: unsealed with LOAD/STORE; object: sealed without EXECUTE; call gate: sealed with EXECUTE; type capability: unsealed with PERMIT_SEAL); object types are not addresses (separate otype field); software holding the omnipotent root can create capabilities with arbitrary permission combinations.
assumptions: Orthogonal permission representation (contrast Appendix C.4)
map_note: RP3/RP5: the permission and otype fields are independent coordinates of the authority order; none of the four kinds can be converted to another without the appropriate authority

statement: CHERI-RISC-V new capability exception: a single trap cause with xtval reporting the capability exception code (Table 4.4: Length, Tag, Seal, Type, Software-defined permission, and one per architectural permission) and the index of the offending register (cap idx; MSB selects the SCR file); if more than one capability exception applies, the highest-priority code per Table 4.5 is reported.
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1: the model's trap-value function must be total and deterministic over Table 4.4/4.5; G-c: CVA6-CHERI xtval must refine it

statement: Hybrid privilege: CHERI retains ring-based privilege and additionally allows ambient ring privilege (MMU, cache, interrupt management) to be constrained by permissions on PCC, so that code within a low ring can be prevented from exercising virtual-memory features that would bypass in-kernel sandboxing; 'privilege through capability context' is the authority an execution context holds within an address space without recourse to a lower ring.
assumptions: None
map_note: G-CF: CF compartments inside M/S mode rely on PCC-gated privilege rather than ring changes

statement: RVWMO definition: an execution of a RISC-V program obeys the RVWMO memory consistency model only if there exists a global memory order (a total order over all harts' memory operations) conforming to preserved program order and satisfying the Load Value Axiom, the Atomicity Axiom, and the Progress Axiom.  The appendices give axiomatic (Alloy, Herd) and operational formalisations.
assumptions: Mixed-size overlapping accesses 'subject to revision'; Ztso is a strengthening
source: RISCVInternational-25a §17.1.4 L3996; §17 intro L3832-3844; Appendix B.1/B.2 L860-861
map_note: A-1: the ISA model must be parameterised by a memory model that refines RVWMO; G-c: the CVA6/NPU memory subsystem must witness a global memory order

statement: Preserved program order (PPO): operation a precedes b in PPO (hence in global memory order) if a precedes b in program order, both access regular main memory, and any of: (1) b is a store and they overlap; (2) both loads of a byte x with no intervening store to x returning values from different writes; (3) a is an AMO/SC and b is a load returning a's value; (4) a FENCE orders a before b; (5) a has acquire; (6) b has release; (7) both RCsc; (8) a paired with b; (9) address dependency; (10) data dependency; (11) b is a store with control dependency on a; (12) pipeline load dependency via intermediate store m; (13) pipeline store dependency via intermediate address-dependent m.
assumptions: I/O regions excluded from PPO (ordered via PMAs/fences)
map_note: A-1: the thirteen PPO rules are the obligations for any Sail/Rocq concurrency extension of the AIVHAI model

statement: Load Value Axiom: each byte of each load i returns the value written to that byte by the store that is latest in global memory order among (1) stores to that byte preceding i in global memory order and (2) stores to that byte preceding i in program order (i.e., local store-buffer forwarding is permitted).
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1; G-c5 corollary: a tag must be loaded from the same store that supplied the data bytes, or atomic binding (P-B2-028) is violated

statement: Atomicity Axiom: if r and w are paired load and store from aligned LR and SC in hart h, s is a store to byte x, and r returns a value written by s, then s precedes w in global memory order and no store from another hart to x lies between s and w.  LR/SC pairing also requires: SC fails if the address is outside the most recent LR's reservation set, if another hart's store to the set is observable between LR and SC, if another device writes the bytes accessed by LR, or if another SC intervenes.
assumptions: Aligned LR/SC; a hart holds one reservation
map_note: A-1: capability-width LR/SC variants (CHERI-RISC-V reuses quad-word atomics, v9 §4.3.13) must satisfy the same axiom with the tag included in the atomically updated word (G-c5)

statement: Progress Axiom: no memory operation may be preceded in the global memory order by an infinite sequence of other memory operations.
assumptions: None
map_note: A-1; note this is the only liveness axiom in RVWMO and is distinct from the availability claims AIVHAI keeps separate

statement: Instruction alignment and misaligned-access invariants: IALIGN=32 in the base (16 with C); an instruction-address-misaligned exception is raised on the taken branch or jump, not on the target, and never on a not-taken branch; naturally aligned loads and stores shall not raise an address-misaligned exception and are guaranteed atomic; misaligned accesses may complete, trap as address-misaligned, or trap as access-fault per the EEI, and are not guaranteed atomic; LR/SC and AMOs require natural alignment.
assumptions: EEI-defined behaviour for misaligned data access
map_note: A-1: instruction-level preconditions the Sail model must encode; G-c5: aligned capability-width accesses inherit the atomicity guarantee, misaligned ones do not

statement: Trap taxonomy: contained, requested, invisible, and fatal traps; the EEI defines per trap whether it is handled precisely, with preciseness recommended where possible; contained and requested traps can be observed to be imprecise by software.  PMP violations are always trapped precisely; PMA violations are strongly recommended to trap precisely but may surface as imprecise bus-error interrupts.
assumptions: None
map_note: G-c: the CVA6-CHERI refinement must state which traps are precise; a non-bypass argument needs PMP (and capability) faults precise so no partial effect escapes

statement: PMP checking scope: PMP checks apply to all accesses whose effective privilege is S or U, including instruction fetch and data accesses in S/U, M-mode data accesses when mstatus.MPRV=1 with MPP in {S,U}, and page-table accesses for translation (effective privilege S); optionally to M-mode accesses, in which case the entries are locked until reset.  PMP can grant permissions to S/U (which have none by default) and revoke from M (which has all by default).  Fetch without X raises instruction access-fault; load/LR without R raises load access-fault; store/SC/AMO without W raises store access-fault.
assumptions: PMP optional; 0, 16, or 64 entries; CSRs M-mode only, WARL
map_note: G-CF: PMP is the firmware's physical-address backstop under the capability layer; also the only mechanism guarding page-table memory (cf. P-B2-038)

statement: PMP priority and matching: entries are statically prioritised; the lowest-numbered entry matching any byte of an access determines success or failure; the matching entry must match all bytes of the access or the access fails irrespective of L/R/W/X; with a full match, if L is clear and the mode is M the access succeeds, otherwise it succeeds only if the R/W/X bit for the access type is set; if no entry matches an M-mode access it succeeds; if no entry matches an S/U access and at least one entry is implemented, it fails.  A single instruction may generate multiple accesses that are not mutually atomic, so part of a misaligned store may become visible before the fault.
assumptions: TOR with pmpaddr[i-1] >= pmpaddr[i] matches nothing; granularity G is platform-wide
map_note: G-CF: a deterministic, checkable decision procedure; the partial-visibility clause is a residual that an isolation proof must handle (effects before a fault)

statement: PMP locking: when L is set, writes to pmpcfg_i and pmpaddr_i are ignored (and to pmpaddr_{i-1} if A=TOR) until the hart is reset, and R/W/X are enforced on all privilege modes including M; when L is clear, any M-mode access matching the entry succeeds and R/W/X apply only to S/U.
assumptions: Without Smepmp
map_note: G-CF: locked entries are the only PMP state that survives a compromised M-mode; the firmware proof can rely on them as constants after boot

statement: PMP synchronisation: translations and PMP checks may be performed speculatively and cached; after writing PMP CSRs, M-mode software must execute SFENCE.VMA with rs1=x0 and rs2=x0 to synchronise PMP settings with the virtual memory system and any PMP or address-translation caches (plus HFENCE requirements under H).
assumptions: None
map_note: G-CF: a firmware ordering obligation; omission is a bypass window; A-1: the model needs an explicit fence-to-PMP-visibility rule

statement: Smepmp definitions and MML (Machine Mode Lockdown, sticky until PMP reset): pmpcfg.L now marks a rule M-mode-only (enforced on M, denied in S/U, locked) when set and S/U-mode-only (enforced on S/U, denied on M) when clear; RW=01 and LRWX=1111 encode Shared-Region rules with fixed semantics; adding an executable M-mode-only or locked shared rule is impossible (writes ignored) unless mseccfg.RLB is set; executing with M-mode privileges is only possible from a matching M-mode-only rule or a locked executable Shared-Region, and execution from a region with no matching rule or an S/U-only rule is denied.
assumptions: mseccfg reset value implementation-specific; truth table §6.2.1
map_note: G-CF: the M-mode code-integrity invariant (M executes only from locked, non-writable regions) is a precondition for trusting CF code pages; a checkable rule set

statement: Smepmp MMWP and RLB: MMWP (sticky) changes the M-mode default for addresses with no matching rule from ignored to denied; RLB=1 permits editing locked rules, but if RLB=0 and any entry has L=1 then RLB stays 0 and further writes are ignored until PMP reset; a PMP reset re-initialises all PMP state including locked rules to safe defaults before releasing the hart.
assumptions: RLB intended for boot/debug only
map_note: G-CF: after boot (MMWP=1, MML=1, RLB=0 with some L set) the PMP configuration is immutable, which is what lets a firmware proof treat PMP as a constant

statement: Trap entry/return invariant: each mode x that handles interrupts has a two-level stack xPIE/xPP; when a trap is taken from mode y into mode x, xPIE := xIE, xIE := 0, xPP := y (xPP can only hold modes up to x); on xRET, xIE := xPIE, privilege := xPP, xPIE := 1, xPP := least-privileged supported mode.  mepc/sepc are written with the virtual address of the interrupted or faulting instruction and mcause/scause with the cause, only when a trap is taken; otherwise never written by the implementation.
assumptions: Hypervisor extension adds V/MPV/SPV handling (§21.6.2)
map_note: G-CF: the exception path is one of the two non-monotonic transitions; its privilege bookkeeping must be modelled exactly (A-1) and refined by CVA6-CHERI (G-c)

statement: Synchronous exception priority: if an instruction may raise multiple synchronous exceptions, Table 15 (decreasing priority) determines which is taken: instruction address breakpoint highest; ... ; load/store/AMO address-misaligned lowest, except that misaligned may have either higher or lower priority than load/store/AMO page-fault and access-fault (implementation-defined); instruction-address-misaligned has lower priority than other instruction-address exceptions because it is raised by the control-flow instruction; custom, software-check and hardware-error exception priorities are extension- or implementation-defined.
assumptions: Interrupts take precedence over synchronous exceptions per §3.1.9
map_note: A-1: the base priority order that CHERI-RISC-V's Table 4.5 must be spliced into (capability faults above alignment and MMU faults); G-c: CVA6-CHERI's priority encoder must refine the combined order

statement: Trap value: on trap into M-mode, mtval is set to zero or exception-specific information; the platform specifies which exceptions must set it informatively; when page-based virtual memory is enabled, mtval holds the faulting virtual address even for physical-memory access faults; mtval is never written by the implementation except on trap.
assumptions: Platform-defined informativeness
map_note: A-1: CHERI-RISC-V overloads xtval with capability cause/index (P-B2-075); the model must define the combined encoding

statement: Virtual address translation (Sv32/39/48 algorithm): satp must be active (effective S or U); each PTE access is PMA/PMP-checked (access-fault on violation); invalid PTE, R=0 and W=1, or reserved bits set raise page-fault; non-leaf descent with i<0 raises page-fault; misaligned superpage raises page-fault; U-bit check against mode/SUM/MXR, shadow-stack check (access-fault), then R/W/X check (page-fault); A/D update either faults (Svade) or is performed atomically with a PMA/PMP check on the PTE store, retrying from step 2 if the compare fails; an implementation may not split an 8-byte PTE read into two 4-byte reads.
assumptions: Address-translation caches are read-only, incoherent, per-hart, flushed by SFENCE.VMA
map_note: A-1: the walker algorithm is a stepwise specification the model must implement literally; G-CF: page-table memory is guarded only by PMP/PMA, so firmware isolation depends on PMP (P-B2-084) and on the capability layer not covering the walker (P-B2-038)

statement: Speculative translation constraints: speculative executions of the address-translation algorithm behave as non-speculative ones except that they must not set the dirty bit, must not trigger an exception, and must not create address-translation cache entries that would have been invalidated by any SFENCE.VMA executed since the speculation began; multiple cache entries may co-exist for one address (the choice between old and new PTE is unpredictable but otherwise well-defined); A/D bits may only be updated in memory directly.
assumptions: None
map_note: G-c: an RTL obligation on CVA6's MMU; A-1: the model's TLB nondeterminism must be bounded exactly this way

statement: CSR access ordering: CSR accesses are weakly ordered under RVWMO and are not ordered with respect to explicit memory accesses unless the CSR access modifies the execution behaviour of the memory-accessing instruction, or a syntactic dependency or Memory-Ordering PMA orders them; otherwise a FENCE is required.
assumptions: Note says this should move into chapter 17
map_note: A-1: CSpecialRW on DDC/PCC-affecting state 'modifies the execution behaviour' of subsequent loads, so the model must order it; G-c: CVA6-CHERI's non-forwarded SCR path (v9 §11.1.3) is one realisation

statement: mtvec: when MODE=Direct all traps into M-mode set pc to BASE; when MODE=Vectored synchronous exceptions set pc to BASE and interrupts set pc to BASE + 4 x cause.  (CHERI-RISC-V extends mtvec to MTCC; the CSR view is the SCR's address.)
assumptions: None
map_note: G-CF: the handler entry set is finite and fixed by MTCC, which is what makes 'known entry points' (P-B2-058 clause a) checkable

statement: The Sail CHERI-RISC-V model is the source of the instruction pseudocode in the specification: the document states that the CHERI-RISC-V pseudocode is derived from the Sail CHERI-RISC-V model, and the Sail descriptions of CHERI-MIPS and CHERI-RISC-V are used for formal proof, SMT checking, and are directly incorporated into the ISA specification.
assumptions: Chapter 7 'Semantics' blocks are generated, not hand-written
source: WatsonNeumannWoodruffEtAl-23 front matter L58; §12.9 L10395; §6 L4402
map_note: A-1: for CHERI-RISC-V the specification and the Sail model are the same artifact by construction, so 'model matches spec' reduces to provenance of the generated text plus the prose-only clauses catalogued above

statement: CHERI-x86-64 and Morello are sketches/external: CHERI ISA v9 removed CHERI-MIPS, synchronised with Morello, made CHERI-RISC-V the primary reference platform, stores capabilities in general-purpose registers, clears tags for non-monotonic modifications, and disables DDC/PCC relocation by default (ccsr.nr=1).
assumptions: Version-history statement
map_note: A-1: fixes which design the AIVHAI Sail model is held to (CHERI-RISC-V v9 semantics, tag-clearing, no relocation); the CHERI-MIPS proofs in [114] were against a design no longer in the document

statement: Threat model: the attacker may execute arbitrary instructions and measure timing differences (FLUSH+RELOAD), but 'it should not be possible for attackers to gain privileges nor to leak any secret - even if only through transient execution'.
assumptions: Attacker constrained to RISC-V privilege level and address space; cache side channels themselves need not be prevented by hardware (software takes measures, following AMD SEV-SNP and Arm whitepaper)
source: FuchsWoodruffMooreEtAl-21, Sec. 3 Security and Threat Model, L156
map_note: none; a microarchitectural attacker model, outside the architectural refinement obligations

statement: CHERI systems are expected to respect the security model of the baseline ISA (RISC-V): attackers should not execute code in a more-privileged level nor access another address space unless explicitly granted.
assumptions: Baseline ISA is RISC-V with M/S/U privilege levels
map_note: G-c; CVA6-CHERI must preserve RISC-V privilege and address-space isolation as a consequence of refining the RVY model, though the paper's concern is its transient-execution extension

statement: Assumption: cache side channels do not need to be prevented by hardware; software has to take appropriate measures.
assumptions: Follows AMD SEV-SNP [8] and Arm [1]
map_note: none; side channels are defence-in-depth outside the AIVHAI formal boundary

statement: 'CHERI systems must not allow access beyond existing capability bounds and permissions - even if only in transient execution'; several tests in the suite prove the absence (or presence) of this property.
artifact: other: bare-metal assembly test suite (github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/Test-Suite-Transient-Execution), verilator + VCU-118 FPGA
assumptions: Bare-metal, no OS; FLUSH+RELOAD oracle
map_note: G-c; the strongest transient-execution reading of bounds/permission enforcement that a CVA6-CHERI refinement of the RVY model would need to extend to speculative accesses

statement: Test oracle: 'An attack is successful if it can leak a secret value'; all attacks use the FLUSH+RELOAD cache-timing side channel; the probed cache line that was touched is accessed at 23 cycles versus more than 66 for the others.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator simulation and VCU-118 FPGA
assumptions: Software flush loop (no RISC-V/RiscyOO flush instruction); cache state predictable because the attack is the only code running
source: FuchsWoodruffMooreEtAl-21, Sec. 2.1 L84-86, Sec. 4 L162, Fig. 1 L97-99
map_note: none; a leak oracle for microarchitectural testing, not an architectural property

statement: Verilator simulation behaves similarly in memory delays to the VCU-118 FPGA implementation, 'which makes our simulation results credible for future attack results'.
artifact: other: verilator vs FPGA cache-probe timing comparison
assumptions: Same configuration parameters in simulation and synthesis (Table 1)
map_note: none; a methodological validation of the simulation platform

statement: Spectre-PHT (RISC-V variant) is successful on RiscyOO: PHT mistraining lets attacker-controlled i speculatively read array0 out of bounds and encode it via array1.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: OoO superscalar, n=2, 64-entry OoO window; bare-metal
map_note: none; a vulnerability finding on RiscyOO, not a CVA6 property

statement: Spectre-PHT (CHERI-RISC-V variant) is unsuccessful on CHERI RiscyOO when the capability guarding array0 is bounded to exactly size elements, because 'it is not possible to transiently access memory out of capability bounds in CHERI RiscyOO'; 'if array0's capability grants access to more than size elements, a successful Spectre-PHT attack on CHERI RiscyOO is possible'.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: Depends on the concrete capability configuration; CHERI compiler establishes bounds from allocations
map_note: G-c; a transient-execution consequence of bounds checks being completed before memory issue, which CVA6-CHERI's memory pipeline would have to reproduce

statement: Spectre-BTB is successful on both RISC-V and CHERI-RISC-V variants: attacker gadgets executed in S privilege mode and kernel capabilities leaked to attacker gadgets, because the 1024-entry hashed BTB aliases and, in CHERI RiscyOO, 'the BTB stores not just the target address, but the entire target capability' including its validity tag.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: BTB with hash-induced collisions; attacker can insert an entry by executing a branch to the gadget
map_note: none; RiscyOO-specific BTB design finding

statement: Spectre-RSB is successful on both variants: 'The RSB stores the entire target capability enabling speculation to powerful capabilities in CHERI RiscyOO'; attacker creates a mismatch between the software stack and the RSB.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: RSB stores full capabilities
map_note: none; RiscyOO-specific RSB design finding

statement: Spectre-STL is successful on both variants: 'a load will be executed out-of-order as soon as all of its arguments are ready', so a load runs before a delayed dependent store; 'CHERI does not put any constraints on store-to-load dependencies, nor on memory versioning'.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: Store address delayed (e.g., fetched from memory); memory disambiguation speculation present
map_note: none; memory-disambiguation speculation is outside the CHERI architectural model by the paper's own account

statement: Meltdown-US is unsuccessful (microarchitecturally prevented): the PTE from the TLB is checked for supervisor-only access in the final stage of the memory execution pipeline, a page fault is raised and handled immediately, and 'the load attempting to fetch a secret will never leave the core'.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: Permission check before issue in the ExeMem/FinishMem stages (Fig. 4)
source: FuchsWoodruffMooreEtAl-21, Table 2 L170, Sec. 4 L188, Fig. 4 L182-184
map_note: none; a RiscyOO pipeline-ordering property, though the same check-before-issue ordering is what CVA6-CHERI would be examined for

statement: Meltdown-US-CHERI (access without a valid capability to the region) is unsuccessful: capability checks are performed in the penultimate stage of the memory execution pipeline; 'In case the capability pointer is out-of-bounds or the capability is invalid, an exception will be raised and the load will not leave the core'.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: Capability bounds/tag check completed before the memory request issues
map_note: G-c; the check-before-issue ordering for capability-authorised loads is the transient-execution form of the RVY bounds/tag check CVA6-CHERI must implement

statement: Meltdown-GP is unsuccessful: privileged system-register permissions are checked in the Rename stage of the in-order front-end; an unprivileged access is marked 'executed' in its ROB entry and is never scheduled to an execution pipeline.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: In-order front-end performs CSR permission check
map_note: none; RiscyOO front-end property

statement: Meltdown-GP-CHERI (speculative read of a Special Capability Register without the Access System Registers permission) is unsuccessful for the same reason: the ASR permission for SCRs is checked in Rename and the instruction is never scheduled.
artifact: other: bare-metal test suite, verilator + VCU-118
assumptions: ASR bit governs SCR access; check in the in-order front-end
source: FuchsWoodruffMooreEtAl-21, Table 2 L173, Sec. 4 L186, L194
map_note: G-c; the ASR permission check is an RVY-level rule whose transient-execution ordering CVA6-CHERI would need to honour

statement: Write-variant Spectre-PHT (speculative buffer overflow to overwrite a return address) is mitigated by CHERI: 'A data write can never lead to valid capability being formed, because the tag bit will be stripped when writing to memory'.
assumptions: Architectural tag-stripping on data stores; argued, not shown by a test
map_note: G-c5; relies on tag integrity in memory (data writes clear tags) holding also for speculative stores

statement: Spectre-PHT does not violate CHERI's security model as long as the attacker accesses only memory granted by the authorizing capability, but it 'breaks the software's guarantee that memory can be guarded by an if statement'.
assumptions: Secure program requires as tight a capability configuration as possible
map_note: none; a scoping statement about what CHERI's architectural model does and does not cover

statement: CHERI-128 compressed bounds can be imprecise, so a capability may grant access to more memory than the data needs, 'which in turn opens the door to Spectre-PHT attacks'.
assumptions: CHERI Concentrate compressed-bounds format
map_note: A-1; bounds imprecision is an encoding-level consequence of the capability format the ISA model must represent faithfully

statement: Spectre-BTB and Spectre-RSB 'clearly violate both the CHERI and the RISC-V security model': speculative jumps are not limited to the current privilege level nor the current compartment, giving access to S-mode privileges (e.g., satp) or powerful capabilities.
assumptions: Mitigations left to future work
map_note: none; RiscyOO finding; no mitigation specified here

statement: Spectre-STL does not violate CHERI's security model: all transient memory accesses are allowed by their capabilities; 'CHERI's security model does not include versions of memory'.
assumptions: Memory versioning outside the architectural model
map_note: none; explicitly outside the CHERI architectural model

statement: 'In order to enforce CHERI's security model, CHERI implementations need to ensure that an attacker never has access to more capabilities than architecturally present.'
assumptions: Applies even in speculation
map_note: G-c; the informal precursor of the 2024 CSC, i.e., speculative behaviour must stay within the architecturally reachable capability set

statement: Proposed but unimplemented mitigation: tag BTB and RSB entries, e.g., with Compartment Identifiers (CIDs), to prevent unauthorized memory accesses and privilege escalation without degrading performance.
assumptions: Not implemented; performance impact unmeasured
map_note: none; a design suggestion only

statement: Test-suite property: all tests run bare-metal without an OS, in RISC-V and CHERI-RISC-V assembly, in simulation and on FPGA while designing RTL, so they 'detect properties of the microarchitecture rather than effects by the operating system'.
artifact: other: bare-metal assembly test suite (verilator, FPGA)
assumptions: OS noise excluded; results also intended to compare against compiler-generated code (CHERI-LLVM)
map_note: none; a validation-methodology statement

statement: Assumption: in experiments the cache state was predictable because the attack was the only code on the processor; real-world attacks would need a probabilistic approach but 'would nevertheless be successful'.
assumptions: Single bare-metal program; software eviction loop with Table 1 parameters
map_note: none; experimental assumption

statement: Microarchitectural configuration under test: RiscyOO with n=2 (two ALU pipelines, one FPU pipeline, one memory pipeline, 2-superscalar), 32 KiB L1 I/D, 1 MiB L2, out-of-order window 64, memory queue size 38; CHERI RiscyOO uses 128-bit capabilities.
assumptions: Same parameters in simulation and synthesis
map_note: none; configuration record

statement: Default CHERI compiler behaviour (attaching bounds to pointers from allocations) mitigates certain attack classes, and those bounds 'were found to be enforced in transient execution' on CHERI RiscyOO.
assumptions: Bounds tight to the object
map_note: G-c; transient enforcement of architectural bounds

statement: 'the CHERI-RISC-V instruction set does not imply defenses against transient execution attacks'; the CHERI RiscyOO microarchitecture 'was not natively safer than its RiscyOO ancestor', though it can mitigate one of the four Spectre attacks.
assumptions: Six attack classes plus two CHERI adaptations
map_note: none; a scoping conclusion about the ISA

statement: Attack precondition: transient-execution attacks rely on misspeculation remaining undetected for as many cycles as possible; increasing load latency by evicting cache lines is essential to the reproductions.
assumptions: Long-latency branch-condition loads
map_note: none; attack technique

statement: Architectural threat model: 'any value that can enter the core ... in speculation is accessible through a side-channel'; the contracts therefore constrain speculative memory accesses and execution paths rather than enumerating side channels.
assumptions: Side-channel mechanisms not modelled individually
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. II, L78-80; Sec. IV L96
map_note: none; threat-model definition

statement: Definition of 'the core': from the execution pipeline to the load/store queue, excluding the L1 caches; the model 'assumes unused bytes of cache lines cannot leak, and that the cache itself, including any prefetching, does not perform data-dependent operations sufficient to create side-channels', and ignores asynchronous agents such as the page-table walker and DMA engines.
assumptions: Single core implied; no DMA, no PTW, no prefetcher leakage considered
map_note: none; explicitly excludes DMA, which is the AIVHAI NPU crux, so the contract's scope does not reach the shim

statement: Vocabulary: an instruction is fetched if in the front-end (need not modify predictor state); executed when data-dependent action is taken (may modify predictor state and access data caches); a branch conditionally affects control flow (excluding exceptions/interrupts); an event is non-speculative if all previous branches have executed; transient if it occurred speculatively but did not commit.
assumptions: In-order front-end flushed at lower cost than the OoO back end
map_note: none; definitions

statement: The contracts are architecture-independent and mapped here to RISC-V; mapping to other ISAs is future work.
assumptions: RISC-V mapping only
map_note: none; scoping

statement: Translation Speculation Contract (TSC): 'All instruction and data-memory operations issued in speculation must be mapped in the page table, and allowed by current page permissions.' RiscyOO natively enforced TSC at full performance.
assumptions: Generator did not detect a violation; see C056 for the oracle
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-C L118-122; Sec. VIII-A L255; Sec. IX L302
map_note: G-c; the speculative strengthening of page-permission enforcement that a CVA6-CHERI refinement would need if it covers issued accesses

statement: Meltdown violates TSC; 'the Meltdown vulnerability could be attributed purely to a lack of this architectural speculation contract'.
assumptions: Many high-performance implementations avoid it without performance penalty
map_note: none; attribution argument

statement: BSC item 1: 'Direct jumps (unconditional with immediate target) will be followed in speculative execution only by the jump target.' Already enforced in RiscyOO (misprediction detected in Decode when the target is known) and tested with Execute-stage assertions.
assumptions: Custom counters in the Execute stage register implausible predicted nextPC
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-D L134-152; Sec. VIII-B L261-263; Sec. IX L315
map_note: none; control-flow speculation contract beyond the RVY model

statement: BSC item 2: 'Direct branches (conditional with immediate target) will be followed in speculative execution only by one of the two possible targets.' Already enforced in RiscyOO (dedicated direction predictor in Decode; implausible prediction flushes fetch) and tested.
assumptions: Foundational for current Spectre mitigations (PHT may mispredict direction but not select an arbitrary BTB target)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-D L148-154, L178; Sec. VIII-B L261-263; Sec. IX L315
map_note: none; control-flow speculation contract beyond the RVY model
