statement: BSC item 3: 'Instructions that cause exceptions will be followed in speculative execution only by the non-faulting path.' A counter for faulting instructions predicting a PC other than the next instruction recorded no events: 'BSC constraint 3 is held by RiscyOO'.
assumptions: At least 94.96% of exception tests raised an exception (front-end, Rename, ALU, or memory)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-D L156, L180; Sec. VIII-B L282; Sec. VIII-D L290
map_note: none; control-flow speculation contract beyond the RVY model

statement: BSC item 4: 'Indirect branches (register target) will be followed in speculative execution only by previous architectural indirect-branch targets from the current compartment.' RiscyOO VIOLATED it: a transient jalr after a csrci (which flushes the pipeline) trained the BTB so that the srliw target executed speculatively after the flush.
assumptions: Searchable vector of committed indirect-jump targets; wild-jump counter; generators bound the number of targets
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-D L158, L182; Sec. VIII-B L265-271, L292-296
map_note: none; BTB training policy, outside the RVY model

statement: BSC item 4 corollary: indirect branches must not default to straight-line prediction; RiscyOO did so when no BTB entry was found, which is 'an exploitable vulnerability in commercial processor implementations'; fixed by pausing fetch until a real redirection arrives from Execute.
assumptions: Decode may predict a guaranteed-invalid address when no previous target exists
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-D L182; Sec. IX L321; Fig. 2 L307
map_note: none; predictor policy

statement: BSC item 5: 'Returns will be followed in speculative execution only by the instruction after a previous call from the current compartment.' RiscyOO VIOLATED it: the RSB was pushed and popped in Decode from the speculative stream, so flushed jumps introduced non-architectural return targets (one class of counterexamples from RSB training in speculation).
assumptions: Record of previous call sites; wild-return counter
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IV-D L160, L184; Sec. VIII-B L265, L280, L298; Sec. IX L323
map_note: none; RSB policy

statement: BSC constrains execution, not fetch: the front-end may speculate freely until decode; 'Allowing wild instruction fetch assumes that it is not possible to leak the contents of memory through the front-end of the pipeline. This should at least require constant-time decoding.'
assumptions: Constant-time decode; no leakage via instruction fetch
map_note: none; explicit assumption of the contract

statement: Memory Ordering Speculation Contract (MOSC): 'Speculatively executed loads will return a value that has been held in that address while in this compartment. Speculatively stored values may be loaded from this compartment; only committed (non-transient) values may be loaded from other compartments.' No other form of data-value speculation is allowed. RiscyOO upholds MOSC (no counterexample).
assumptions: Software must be careful about memory initialization; memory pre-filled with zeros in tests
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. V L170-172, L186-188; Sec. VIII-C L286
map_note: none; value-speculation contract beyond the RVY model

statement: BSC 'does not natively prevent Spectre-PHT attacks that use a transient wrong path to bypass security checks', but guarantees that common software mitigations such as pointer masking will be effective.
assumptions: Intra- and inter-compartment Spectre-PHT remain possible (Table I)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. VI-A, L198, Table I L202-211
map_note: none; scoping of the contract's guarantees

statement: BSC limits Spectre-BTB/RSB: attackers can train BTB and RSB only with architectural targets from the same compartment and cannot inject targets into another compartment; intra-compartment mistraining to previously committed local targets remains possible ('limited'); a compartment can enumerate all speculative targets by analysing only its own code.
assumptions: Compartment switch is visible to the microarchitecture
map_note: none; contract consequence

statement: MOSC prevents inter-compartment Spectre-STL 'if secrets are cleared before memory is shared between domains'.
assumptions: Software clears secrets before sharing
map_note: none; contract consequence with a software precondition

statement: TSC 'fully mitigates Meltdown-US attacks' and also prevents Foreshadow.
assumptions: ISA-specific Meltdown variants (e.g., Meltdown-NM) deliberately not covered
map_note: none; contract consequence

statement: Both TSC and MOSC prevent MDS attacks: TSC against data forbidden by translation/permissions; MOSC by excluding all data-value speculation (including undefined data) other than memory reordering returning data of the same address and compartment.
assumptions: Argued, not tested against MDS gadgets
map_note: none; contract consequence

statement: Assumption: compartments (privilege rings, address spaces, or finer units) must be expressed architecturally and the microarchitecture 'needs to be made aware of the compartment change'; mechanisms for that are future research.
assumptions: Compartment granularity left open
map_note: none; open assumption

statement: Platform under test: Toooba fork of RiscyOO, SMALL configuration: fetch/commit two per cycle, 64-instruction OoO window, two integer, one memory, one FP pipeline with 16-entry issue queues, 38 outstanding memory transactions, 32 KiB 8-way L1s, 1 MiB 16-way L2.
assumptions: Bluespec SystemVerilog; compressed instructions and debug support added over RiscyOO
map_note: none; configuration record

statement: Transient-vulnerability profile: 'All basic Spectre attacks are possible on RiscyOO'; an indirect branch waiting on its target from memory 'can allow more than 28 predicted instructions to execute before flushing on misprediction'.
artifact: other: prior test suite [29][30] and this work
assumptions: SMALL configuration
map_note: none; RiscyOO finding

statement: RiscyOO is vulnerable to BTB aliasing attacks, particularly when using hashed BTB tags.
assumptions: Hashed BTB tags
map_note: none; RiscyOO finding

statement: RiscyOO's PHT is vulnerable to mistraining, 'but only to one of the legitimate targets of the branch'.
assumptions: Direction-only misprediction
map_note: none; RiscyOO finding

statement: RiscyOO's memory subsystem is vulnerable to Spectre Store-To-Load (STL).
assumptions: Memory disambiguation speculation
map_note: none; RiscyOO finding

statement: Meltdown attacks could not be reproduced on RiscyOO 'because page permissions are checked before issuing to memory (Meltdown-US) ... and because system register permissions are checked in the Rename stage before instructions are issued (Meltdown-GP)'.
assumptions: Check-before-issue ordering
map_note: none; RiscyOO finding

statement: Testing method: directed-random test generation in TestRIG using the RISC-V Formal Interface (RVFI) architectural trace plus Hardware Performance Monitoring (HPM) counters as 'a portable bridge between architectural state and the speculative behavior guaranteed by our contracts'; contrasted with IntroSpectre's inconclusive, non-portable debug-trace approach.
assumptions: Arranging scenarios where counters reliably indicate violations was sometimes complex; portable to implementations sharing the same contracts
map_note: none; validation methodology (TestRIG/RVFI) that AIVHAI could reuse but no CVA6 property

statement: TSC test oracle: a page table with one code page and one data page; the data-cache miss counter registers any access outside these pages; random memory instructions attempt disallowed pages; 91.56% of TSC tests triggered a memory exception for insufficient privileges; no TSC violation detected.
assumptions: D-cache miss counter as leak proxy
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. VIII-A L255; Sec. VIII-D L290
map_note: none; test design

statement: BSC jump test oracle: custom assertions with counters in the Execute stage flag an implausible predicted nextPC for direct jumps/branches; a searchable vector of committed indirect-jump targets counts wild predictions; recorded call sites count wild returns; any non-conforming branch is counted as a 'wild jump'; 9.32% of BSC jump tests generated a BTB misprediction.
assumptions: Requires a small amount of added microarchitectural state; generators create instruction cycles with jumps at fixed offsets to bound target counts
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. VIII-B L261-269; Sec. VIII-D L290
map_note: none; test design

statement: MOSC test oracle: state tracks past stores and counts a 'wild load' if a load returns an unseen value; memory initially zero so zero or any recorded prior store value is allowed; random load/store sequences intermixed with other instruction classes.
assumptions: Value-set oracle rather than ordering oracle
map_note: none; test design

statement: BSC enforcement mechanism: predictor (BTB and PHT) training is delayed until the training branch is non-speculative by converting the branch training queue into a SpecFIFO (speculative state tagged by in-flight branches; tag 0 means non-speculative; failed speculation disappears via the branch-resolution broadcast network).
assumptions: Protecting PHT direction data is not essential for BSC; effect on predictor accuracy left to future research
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IX, L302, L313, L317-319; Fig. 2a L307
map_note: none; RiscyOO-specific enforcement

statement: BSC-5 enforcement: roll back the RSB stack pointer on redirection (reduced RSB mispredictions by roughly 90% in CoreMark) and delay RSB writes in the training SpecFIFO so only non-speculative targets are written.
assumptions: RSB push delay is the most expensive component
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IX, L323; Fig. 2b L307
map_note: none; RiscyOO-specific enforcement

statement: Redirection protection for BSC-4/5: Instruction Fetch may proceed on a speculative redirection but Decode is blocked until the redirecting instruction is non-speculative, enforced by a zero-data SpecFIFO holding the speculative state of the last redirection; 'appears to block only very rarely'.
assumptions: BSC guarantees semantics of execution, not fetch
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. IX, L325-341; Fig. 2c L307
map_note: none; RiscyOO-specific enforcement

statement: Exception mistraining: 'To prevent mistraining predictors during an exception, we would use coarser measures (such as flushing) that are a secondary concern for common-case performance.'
assumptions: Not evaluated
map_note: none; design intent

statement: The BSC enforcement mechanisms were re-tested with the same generators, 'which helped identify stray violations and also helped ensure the test routines themselves were flagging appropriate violations'.
assumptions: Mutual validation of enforcement and tests
map_note: none; validation closure

statement: Performance of BSC enforcement on SPECInt2006: without the RSB push delay, execution time improves by 1.2% with a mean 6.9% reduction in redirections (transient training removed); with the RSB push delay, mean 1.8% cycle overhead; overall range -1.2% to +1.8%.
assumptions: SPECInt2006 subset; prototype enforcement
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Abstract L34; Sec. X L347-353; Fig. 3 L330-337
map_note: none; performance evidence

statement: Scoping: the ISA-level contracts 'do not categorically prevent side channels, but enable sound reasoning about software with respect to safety against classes of transient-execution attacks'.
assumptions: Side channels out of scope
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-23, Sec. I L46; Sec. IV L96
map_note: none; scoping

statement: Speculation contracts are stated to be 'particularly necessary for security architectural extensions ... and upcoming extensions such as CHERI'.
assumptions: Motivation for the 2024 CSC
map_note: none; motivation

statement: Threat model: the attacker has arbitrary code execution and observes timing via the cache hierarchy and other side channels; attacker and victim 'are architecturally isolated using CHERI capabilities'; the victim does not collaborate; 'no visibility of failed speculation in the attacker can reveal a secret from the victim'.
assumptions: Intra-address-space compartments; covert channels excluded
map_note: none; threat model, though it is the closest published analogue to AIVHAI's mutually distrusting tenant model

statement: Definition: a value is part of the committed register state 'if the instruction producing this value is non-squashable', i.e., guaranteed to commit even if not yet at the Commit stage.
assumptions: Out-of-order pipeline; chosen to maximise microarchitectural freedom
map_note: none; definition

statement: Definition: a memory access is 'issued' if its address selects data at any level (load queue, store buffer, or L1 data cache); from then on it may index those structures.
assumptions: Includes store-to-load forwarding paths
map_note: none; definition

statement: CHERI invariant 1: capabilities are unforgeable; 'capabilities are derived only from capabilities of greater or equal privilege'; naturally enforceable in speculation because pipelines forward values legitimately calculated from register state.
assumptions: Would-be violations must clear the tag or throw an exception (L80)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. II-A L80; Sec. IV L120-124
map_note: G-c; monotonic derivation is an RVY-level property CVA6-CHERI must refine, here extended to speculative forwarding

statement: CHERI invariant 2: 'Memory can be addressed only through a capability describing and authorizing access to that address'; naturally enforceable in speculation 'as capability metadata is bundled with the address and can be verified before issuing requests to memory'.
assumptions: Check before issue
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. II-A L80; Sec. IV L122-124
map_note: G-c; the core authorisation rule the RVY model states and CVA6-CHERI must implement, including for issued speculative accesses

statement: Capability Speculation Contract (CSC): 'All instruction and data-memory accesses issued in speculation must be authorized by capabilities either: 1) in the committed register file; 2) in memory transitively reachable through 1.' A CHERI processor acts, even in speculation, only with rights transitively reachable from its architecturally committed register file.
assumptions: Does not forbid speculation on capabilities, only using speculatively manipulated capabilities outside the transitive closure; side-channel concerns obviated by preventing illegal accesses from issuing
map_note: G-c; the strongest candidate for a speculative strengthening of the CVA6-CHERI refinement obligation (architectural rights bound issued accesses)

statement: Data-CSC requires aggressive enforcement of both memory bounds and capability provenance before data-memory access; bounds may be checked in parallel with translation, which must also succeed before issue.
assumptions: Data values are forwarded results of valid data flow from committed state
map_note: G-c4; every data access (scalar here) must be bounds- and provenance-checked before issue, the rule G-c4 extends to vector/matrix accesses

statement: Instruction-CSC: instruction fetch may be predicted without dependency on committed state, but executed instructions must lie within the committed PCC bounds, constraining execution to the current compartment; enforcement is 'challenging'.
assumptions: Fetch unconstrained; execution constrained
map_note: G-c; PCC bounds enforcement on executed instructions

statement: Instruction-CSC and data-CSC are coupled: a violation of one can lead to a violation of the other, since code capabilities usually also permit data loads; enforcement of both is required.
assumptions: Demonstrated by the cjalr/auipcc/lb.cap counterexample
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. IV L142; Sec. VII-B L238
map_note: none; coupling argument

statement: Security argument (bounds, permissions): direct violations such as an out-of-bounds load 'are trivially excluded by CSC'; transient permission manipulation enabling unsealing is harmless because 'the only advantage of an unsealed capability is to access memory, which is prevented by CSC'.
assumptions: Memory-centric contract
map_note: none; sufficiency argument by hand

statement: Security argument (provenance validity, integrity, monotonicity): 'if no memory access is allowed through fabricated or expanded capabilities, then no advantage can be gained from transiently possessing provenance-breaking or non-monotonic capabilities'.
assumptions: Transient register-to-register violations tolerated
map_note: none; sufficiency argument by hand

statement: Security argument (encapsulation): changing compartments requires executing instructions and accessing data of the new compartment, both requiring memory access, so 'an attacker cannot gain any advantage by unsealing code and data transiently without violating CSC'.
assumptions: Sealing-based compartmentalisation
map_note: none; sufficiency argument by hand

statement: The memory-centric CSC 'is sufficient to uphold CHERI security guarantees while allowing transient register-to-register violations'; the CHERI-Toooba enforcement nevertheless guards all capability transformations, which 'is not likely to be true for all microarchitectures'.
assumptions: Existing CHERI formal proofs are architectural only and 'explicitly do not consider information leaks via timing channels from transient execution or otherwise' (L84)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. II-A L84; Sec. V L171
map_note: none; sufficiency claim, unproven

statement: Platform: CHERI-Toooba (Toooba = RiscyOO plus compressed instructions, debug unit, prefetching; CHERI-RISC-V with full 128-bit capabilities per Rugg), commit width two, 64-instruction OoO window, two integer, one FP, one memory pipeline, 32 KiB 8-way L1s, 1 MiB 16-way L2; FPGA platforms VCU118 and DE10Pro.
assumptions: Single-core configuration implied
map_note: none; configuration record

statement: TestRIG oracle: instruction sequences are injected and traces collected; 'The assertions ... are asserting that architecturally visible state does not change during the execution of a test. If the architecturally visible state changes, a violation of a constraint has been found.'
assumptions: HPM data-cache miss counter is the architecturally visible proxy
map_note: none; test methodology

statement: Data-CSC generator: full reset clears caches; a prelude prepares a capability granting access to a single word and loads it; thereafter 'any cache misses will indicate a memory access not allowed by this capability'; a random stream of capability instructions follows; the miss counter is read; unexpected misses are a violation. Operands: rOneWord, rInvalid (tag-cleared), rDest.
assumptions: Single generator produced examples of all known data-CSC violations
map_note: none; test design

statement: Data-CSC VIOLATION (CBuildCap): 'lb.cap rDest, cDest[0]; cbuildcap cDest, rInvalid, cInvalid; lb.cap rDest, cDest[0]' transiently constructs a valid capability from an untagged value and loads through it; the load misses L1 and increments the miss counter.
assumptions: First lb.cap still waiting to commit
map_note: G-c; a forwarded result observable before its RVY-specified exception check, i.e., an implementation step not matching the ISA step

statement: Further data-CSC VIOLATIONS: variants of CSetBounds (csetbounds, csetboundsexact, csetboundsimmediate), plus CUnseal and CInvoke 'that illegally dereference sealed capabilities in transient execution'.
assumptions: Six counterexample classes in total (Table I)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. VII-A L207; Table I L251-253
map_note: G-c; same forwarded-before-check pattern across bounds and sealing instructions

statement: Root cause (Meltdown-CF, Meltdown Capability Forgery): loads proceed through forwarded capabilities without accounting for exception checks; 'Several crucial CHERI exceptions require a full bounds check, which is not performed until the cycle after the execution result has been forwarded' (ExeALU forwards, FinishALU reports the exception).
artifact: other: manual HDL inspection plus TestRIG
assumptions: Faulting-instruction semantics generally imply a speculative result with late flush, so 'other implementations would follow the same dangerous pattern'
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. VII-A L211-215; Fig. 3 L220-222; Sec. IX-A L320
map_note: G-c; the exact hazard class a CVA6-CHERI implementation review should look for (result forwarded before the capability exception check)

statement: Enforcement requirement for data-CSC: 'an implementation must either perform all capability checks before forwarding the register result, or must develop a new mechanism to prevent issuing memory operations that depend on a pending capability check'.
assumptions: Two admissible strategies
map_note: G-c; implementation obligation for any CHERI pipeline including CVA6-CHERI

statement: Instruction-CSC generator: train the BTB with jumps inside a permissive PCC, restrict the PCC bounds, re-run a similar sequence to trigger mispredictions carrying the permissive bounds; auipcc copies the executing PCC into a register (portable observation without special counters) and lb.cap through it counts unexpected D-cache misses. Counterexample: 'cjalr x0, x23; auipcc x25, 0; lb.cap x24, x25[0]'.
assumptions: Detects executed (not merely fetched) CSC-violating instructions
map_note: none; test design

statement: Instruction-CSC VIOLATION root cause: 'CHERI-Toooba violates instruction-CSC due to predicting the entirety of PCC, including the bounds and permissions' from the BTB, which 'allows transient execution into foreign compartments'.
assumptions: BTB stores full PCC bounds of previous targets
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. VII-B L242; Sec. IX-B L330
map_note: none; CHERI-Toooba BTB design; CVA6-CHERI's PCC handling would need its own check

statement: Generator efficiency: over 2000 runs the data-CSC generator produced a counterexample in 2.55% of runs (cbuildcap 0.10%, csetbounds 0.05%, csetboundsexact 0.20%, csetboundsimmediate 0.20%, cunseal 0.20%, cinvoke 1.80%; skew due to TestRIG shrinking bias); the instruction-CSC generator produced one class at 0.35%.
assumptions: 2000-run sample
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. VII-C, L246-255; Table I L251-253
map_note: none; test statistics

statement: Scope limit: manual inspection of the HDL found no additional sources of CSC violations, but 'our testing is not exhaustive and might have potentially missed some cases'; formally specifying the contracts and exhaustively testing them is future work.
assumptions: No formal specification of CSC exists
map_note: none; explicit non-claim

statement: Meltdown-CF exploit (cbuildcap variant) in a user-mode pure-capability CheriBSD process on CHERI-Toooba (FPGA): two protection domains in one address space; the attacker forges an untagged 128-bit pattern, feeds it to cbuildcap with an insufficient authorizing capability, the hardware 'optimistically sets the tag and forwards this capability', the secret is loaded and encoded via flush+reload; measured 'approximately 1.4 bytes/second ... with an error rate of 0%'.
assumptions: cbuildcap placed under a mispredicted branch whose condition load misses all caches; side-channel buffer evicted with care for lazy page allocation and compiler optimisations
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. VIII, L265-305; code L277-297; Fig. 4 L312
map_note: G-c; end-to-end demonstration that the forwarded-before-check implementation step breaks the architectural spatial-safety guarantee

statement: Mitigation (architectural): change the CHERI-RISC-V specification 'to clear tags on illegal capability manipulations rather than throw exceptions', so 'implementations should reflect failure atomically in the forwarded result, removing the opportunity for transient, illegal capability'; accepted upstream and 'included in current CHERI-RISC-V drafts for ratification'.
assumptions: Responsible disclosure to the CHERI-RISC-V and Morello teams
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Abstract L34; Sec. I L60; Sec. IX-A L322, L326; Conclusion L364
map_note: A-1; tag-clearing semantics are now the specified behaviour the RVY Sail model must agree with

statement: Mitigation (microarchitectural, data-CSC): the entire capability exception check was moved into the ExeALU stage so the forwarded tag reflects any error; 'We verified using our data-CSC TestRIG generator that this change eliminated all known Meltdown-CF violations'; no cycle delays introduced; VCU118 LUT +0.86%, FF -0.5% (within synthesis variation); timing met at 25 MHz (VCU118) and 50 MHz (DE10).
assumptions: A high-performance ASIC 'may need to implement rare capability operations using multiple cycles'
map_note: G-c; the implementation fix that makes the implementation step match the (new) ISA step

statement: Morello already specifies tag-clearing semantics ('inadvertently ... for consistency with the Arm architecture') and reviewed its in-progress microarchitecture after disclosure.
assumptions: No test reported on Morello for Meltdown-CF
map_note: none; Morello statement

statement: In-order core strategy for instruction-CSC: predict only the PCC address and forward the bounds from the last-executed branch, reading and checking bounds in Execute when all previous jumps have executed, which 'incidentally' enforces instruction-CSC.
assumptions: In-order pipeline; PCC bounds not needed in early stages
map_note: none; not an OoO (CVA6-class) recipe

statement: SinglePCC (instruction-CSC enforcement for OoO): predict that PCC bounds did not change; only instructions within the PCC written by the latest-executed branch (itself legal under data-CSC) may execute; all PC bounds state replaced by a single PCC register; 'Any jump to a capability with different bounds will trigger a flush at the Commit stage'; 'We verified that this design eliminates known instruction-CSC vulnerabilities using our TestRIG generators.'
assumptions: Full flush on every cross-bounds jump
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. IX-B, L332-334; Fig. 5 L341
map_note: G-c; executed instructions confined to committed PCC bounds

statement: SinglePCC area: approximately 4.89% fewer LUTs on both boards and 5.48% (DE10Pro) / 6.67% (VCU118) fewer registers, eliminating 'over 15% of the logic required to add CHERI support to the Toooba core'.
assumptions: VCU118 and DE10Pro synthesis
map_note: none; area evidence

statement: SinglePCC performance: 3.43% mean SPECint2006 cycle overhead for full CSC enforcement; fewer than 1.2 extra flushes per 1000 instructions on average; only omnet exceeds 2 flushes/1000 and 5% overhead.
assumptions: Distinct bounds per dynamically loaded library; flush on every cross-library call
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Abstract L34; Sec. IX-B L358; Figs. 6-7 L343, L356
map_note: none; performance evidence

statement: Morello partially enforces instruction-CSC unintentionally: PCC readers block until the previous jump has executed, which prevents wild PCCs from being used for data access 'but still allows wild execution'; measured 10.7% cycle overhead (using an unsafe compiler workaround with legacy integer jumps).
assumptions: Transient-execution mitigation was not a Morello design goal
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. I L66; Sec. IX-B L347-358
map_note: none; Morello comparison

statement: Future optimisation: predict jumps that would change PCC and pause following instructions in Rename until the jump commits ('should cut cycle overhead in half'), or a full bounds-prediction engine that respects committed register state.
assumptions: Not implemented
map_note: none; design suggestion

statement: Claim: 'the CSC specification with the test generator was sufficient to expose serious transient-execution violations and support the development of a safe implementation'; SinglePCC plus early exception check 'provides complete enforcement of CSC in CHERI-Toooba'.
assumptions: 'Complete' relative to known violation classes found by non-exhaustive generators (see C090)
source: FuchsWoodruffRuggEtAl-24, Sec. I L48, L64; Conclusion L364
map_note: none; summary claim

statement: A capability speculation contract 'embodies the transient-execution threat model, enabling testing and even formal verification against clear properties' for microarchitectures, and gives software building blocks for reasoning about transient-execution safety.
assumptions: No formal verification performed in this work
map_note: none; aspiration, not an executed verification

statement: A capability-relative load/store 'will check that the capability ... is a valid capability, check that it has load permission, and check that the range covered ... is all in bounds. If, and only if, all of these checks pass, will it do the ... load. If any of these fail, the instruction will trap.'
artifact: Sail model (ISA semantics); book gives prose only
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 2.2 Understanding CHERI capabilities, approx line 388
map_note: none — this is the access-check rule that RP2/RP3 make meaningful, not itself a monotonicity property; it is the hardware-side premise of G-c

statement: Out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic followed by access traps: 'CHERI says more concretely that it will trap: you are not authorised to access that memory with this capability.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: none — spatial-safety enforcement rule; premise of G-c

statement: 'every pointer in a higher-level language such as C, and every implicit pointer (such as the stack pointer, global pointer, and so on) ... is a CHERI capability.' CHERIoT 'does not have this hybrid mode' and 'assumes all code will be recompiled'.
assumptions: all code recompiled for CHERIoT; no legacy integer-pointer mode
map_note: G-c — purecap-only ABI is a precondition for compartment isolation claims

statement: Tag bit as provenance proof: 'If a memory location or a register has its valid bit set, then it holds a capability and the hardware promises that this was derived from a valid sequence of operations from some more powerful capability.'
artifact: Sail model (SMT-checked properties mentioned but unspecified)
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP1 — this is the monotonicity/provenance guarantee in its most general form

statement: Data writes clear tags: 'If you store data (for example, a 32-bit word or an 8-bit byte) somewhere in a 65-bit chunk, the data will be stored and the tag bit will be cleared.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP4 — direct statement of tag unforgeability via data stores

statement: Atomic tag+data movement: 'Tag bits and their accompanying data are moved between registers and memory atomically. This guarantees that you can't write part of a capability and some data to the same location and end up with a valid capability.'
artifact: none (microarchitectural property; Sail models it as a single step)
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP4 — tag integrity against torn writes; an implementation obligation on the core/memory system

statement: Load-global stripping: 'Any capability loaded via a capability without [load-global] permission will have its global (and load-global) permission stripped. It can then be stored only via a capability that has the store-local permission.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP3 — loaded capability's permissions are narrowed, never widened; also the mechanism behind G-c no-capture

statement: Thread isolation by construction: 'CHERIoT RTOS provides the store-local permission exclusively to stacks and stack capabilities are not global. This combination initially guarantees thread isolation ... Pointers to stack allocations are derived from the stack capability, and so lack global, and can therefore be stored only on the stack.'
assumptions: loader hands store-local only to stacks/trusted stacks (C26-032); no other memory has store-local
map_note: G-c — thread isolation (stack confinement) is the core thread-isolation invariant

statement: Shallow and deep no-capture: removing global means 'The callee cannot hold onto a copy of the pointer after the end of the call' (shallow, callee may capture pointers reachable through the object); removing load-global 'makes this a deep no-capture guarantee: Any pointer loaded, at any level of indirection, from the original pointer ... can be stored only on the stack.'
assumptions: store-local confined to stacks (C26-008)
map_note: G-c — temporal delegation bound; derived from RP3 (C26-007)

statement: Shallow and deep immutability: without store permission 'you cannot use it to modify the object'; removing load-mutable 'turns this into a deep immutability guarantee, stripping both store and load-mutable permissions from any capability that you load.'
artifact: Sail model (load-mutable stripping is ISA semantics)
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP3 — permission narrowing on load; read-only views cannot regain write

statement: 'The access-system-registers permission controls access to a small number of privileged registers and is never handed out to code other than a tiny trusted component in the core of the RTOS.'
assumptions: loader correctness
map_note: G-CF — ASR confinement to the switcher is the firmware privilege boundary

statement: Encoding limitation stated as a rule: 'execute permission implies load. It is not possible to remove load permission from an executable capability.' (12 permissions in 5 bits by excluding meaningless combinations.)
assumptions: CHERIoT 64-bit encoding
map_note: RP3 — the compressed permission lattice constrains which narrowings exist; relevant when porting permission-monotonicity to RVY/64-bit encodings

statement: Compartment-level memory safety target: code from a different security context cannot (1) access objects unless passed pointers, (2) access outside bounds given a valid pointer, (3) access an object or its memory after free, (4) hold a pointer to an on-stack object after the call, (5) hold a temporarily delegated pointer beyond a single call, (6) modify an object passed via immutable reference, (7) modify anything reachable from a deeply immutable reference, (8) tamper with an object passed via opaque reference.
assumptions: 'it's up to the compiler and the RTOS to cooperate'; 'Inline assembly that references the global-pointer or stack-pointer registers directly can bypass spatial memory safety for these objects, but only from within the same compartment'; heap properties require the RTOS shared heap
source: Chisnall-26, 2.5 Building memory safety, approx lines 523-541
map_note: G-c — this eight-point list is the clearest statement of the compartment isolation contract in the book

statement: Sealed capabilities are immutable: 'With a non-zero object type, the sealed capability cannot be modified. Any attempt to change the address, bounds, or permission will clear the tag ... It can be copied but is always treated as an opaque value. Unsealing is the only operation that can modify a sealed capability.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 — sealed-capability opacity; also RP1 (tampering yields untagged, never more authority)

statement: Unseal correctness: unseal 'requires a valid capability with permit-unseal permission and the same address as the capability that was used in the original seal operation. The unseal operation results in a capability that is identical to the one that was sealed.' Unsealing with the wrong key 'you will get back an untagged value'.
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 — sealing round-trip identity and tamper detection

statement: Object-type space is 3 bits in CHERIoT; sealing sets 'the object type of the newly sealed capability to the address of the capability that authorised the seal operation'; for permit-seal/unseal capabilities 'The address field ... refers to the object-type space, rather than the memory address space.'
assumptions: CHERIoT encoding; allocator virtualises sealing beyond 3 bits (C26-073)
source: Chisnall-26, 2.6 approx line 559 and 5.7 approx line 1660
map_note: RP5 — otype encoding; the RVY/64-bit port will have a different otype width, so the virtualised-sealing dependency may change

statement: Sentry semantics: 'A sentry capability can be unsealed automatically by jumping to it. Return addresses are automatically sealed by the jump-and-link instructions, so you cannot modify a return address, you can only jump to it.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 — sentries usable only via jump; return-address integrity

statement: Return-address and forward sentries are distinct kinds: 'If you substitute a return address on the stack with a function pointer (or vice versa) you will get a trap in the jump. This makes control-flow hijacking attacks very hard to mount.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 — sentry-kind discrimination enforced by the jump instruction

statement: Sentry-protected data: 'A sentry can point to a region of memory that contains both code and data. The data is accessible via PC-relative addressing only after jumping into the code.' (Used for cross-compartment calls; gives 'memory that is readable only while executing from it'.)
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 — opacity of sentry targets to the holder

statement: Interrupt-status register 'can be modified only by code running with the Access System Registers permission in the program counter capability.'
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 2.7 Controlling interrupt status, approx line 575
map_note: G-CF — only ASR-bearing (switcher) code may toggle interrupts directly

statement: Interrupt sentries: 'three kinds of sentries that control the interrupt status. These either enable or disable interrupts, or leave the interrupt enabled state untouched. The branch-and-link instruction captures the current exception state in the return sentry.' This 'guarantee[s] that, on return, the interrupt status is reset as it should be'.
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 and G-CF — interrupt state is structured (lexically scoped) via sentry kinds; no 'unstructured' disable

statement: 'A compartment can use [interrupt-disabled library functions] without having the ability to arbitrarily toggle interrupts, giving a limit on the amount of time that it can run with interrupts disabled.'
artifact: hand argument + audit report (interrupt status of each entry point is recorded)
assumptions: interrupt-disabled functions have bounded run time (book warns at 5.4 that an unbounded one 'would guarantee that you would miss your realtime deadlines')
map_note: G-CF — availability: bounded interrupt-disabled execution is auditable, not enforced by hardware

statement: Cross-compartment call state clearing: 'When code in one compartment calls another, it loses access to everything that was not explicitly shared. Specifically: All registers except argument registers are zeroed. The stack capability is truncated to exclude the portion used by the caller. The portion of the stack that is delegated from the caller to the callee is zeroed. On return, the stack becomes accessible again but a similar set of state clearing guarantees confidentiality from the callee to the caller.'
artifact: hand argument (switcher code, 'under 500 instructions', formal verification 'underway')
assumptions: switcher correctness; stack high-water mark used to bound zeroing (C26-086)
source: Chisnall-26, 2.8 Isolating components, approx lines 601-609; 3.2 approx line 707
map_note: G-c — the switcher-enforced confidentiality/integrity contract across compartment transitions

statement: 'At the start of execution, each compartment has a guarantee that nothing else can see or modify its globals. If one compartment passes a pointer to one of its globals to another, you now have shared memory.'
assumptions: initial state only; sharing is by explicit delegation thereafter
map_note: G-c — initial-state confinement of CGP region

statement: Libraries are not a security boundary: library invocation 'doesn't clear the stack or registers'; 'malicious code in the library could inspect or modify everything on the caller's stack'; 'a malicious library can access any globals in the caller'. Conversely 'All entry points exported from a shared library are invoked via sentries', so 'the caller cannot directly read its code or (immutable) data', but library globals 'should not be considered private in a security sense' and on a trap 'the error handler for the caller compartment may see the register file for the middle of the library'.
assumptions: libraries written in a compiled language leak; only 'very careful assembly' can hold secrets
source: Chisnall-26, 2.9 approx line 621; 5.3 approx line 1473; 6 intro approx lines 2131-2135; 6.1 approx line 2149
map_note: G-c — explicit scoping: library boundaries carry no isolation claim; only compartment boundaries do

statement: Pointer provenance: 'Pointers cannot be made up from thin air. When a CHERI system boots, it starts with one or more capabilities in registers that convey the full set of permissions ... there is a chain of derivations that leads back to these initial capabilities ... CHERI doesn't let you reconstruct that chain but it does guarantee that it, or some equivalent chain, must have existed.'
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 3.1 Starting the system with the loader, approx line 665
map_note: RP1 — the sequence-level monotonicity statement (every live capability has a derivation from a root)

statement: 'When a CHERIoT CPU boots, it will have a small set of root capabilities in registers. These, between them, convey the full set of rights that can be granted by a capability. Every capability in the running system is derived (often via many steps) from one of these. As such, the loader is able to do anything.' In multi-stage boot 'the initial capabilities provided to the loader may be restricted'.
assumptions: loader is in the TCB; 'The risk from the loader is mitigated by the fact that it does not run on untrusted data'
map_note: RP1 and G-CF — root-capability authority model; loader is the only holder of roots

statement: Running the loader once (with tag-preserving NVRAM) 'ensures that the initial state for each component's memory contains only capabilities that the loader explicitly grants to it.' Nested bootloaders can be built 'from capabilities and so, unlike systems based on protection rings such as TrustZone, an arbitrary number can be nested.'
assumptions: firmware image embeds no capabilities (provenance flows through the on-device loader)
map_note: G-CF — initial-state capability provisioning is loader-only

statement: Relocation provenance: 'A malicious compartment may provide a relocation that points to a global outside its own memory, but the loader will attempt to derive the capability only from the compartment's initial pcc (code) and cgp (globals) regions and so will fail. Globals may point to other globals owned by the compartment; the loader will fail to derive a valid capability if they point elsewhere.'
artifact: hand argument (loader uses compile-time-checked PermissionSet, 5.10 approx line 1963)
assumptions: loader correctness
map_note: G-c — initial cross-compartment references cannot be forged through relocations

statement: 'The loader operates only on the instructions generated by the linker and so it is possible to audit precisely what it will do ... It is also possible to validate this by running the loader in a simulator and capturing the precise memory state after it has run.'
assumptions: linker report is faithful; reproducible build
map_note: G-CF — loader determinism/auditability; evidence-generation pattern relevant to AIVHAI's proof-boundary

statement: 'The loader enforces some of the guarantees in the initial state. It is structured to be able to enforce some of these by construction. For example, only stacks and trusted stacks (accessible only by the switcher) have store-local permission and these do not have global permission. The [loader] derives these from a capability that has store-local but not global permissions and derives all other capabilities from one that has the store-local permission removed.'
artifact: hand argument (by-construction derivation tree in loader)
assumptions: none beyond loader correctness; note the book says 'scheduler derives' in this sentence, which is almost certainly a typo for loader
map_note: G-CF and G-c — the root split (store-local vs. not) is what makes C26-008 hold

statement: 'Before starting the system, the loader erases almost all of its code (leaving the stub that handles this erasure), its stack, and clears its registers. The last bit of the loader's code becomes the idle thread.' Loader stack becomes scheduler stack; loader code memory becomes heap.
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-CF — root capabilities and loader authority do not survive into steady state

statement: 'The switcher is the only component in a running CHERIoT system that has access-system-registers permission. It uses this primarily to access a single reserved register that holds the capability that defines the trusted stack for the current thread.'
artifact: hand argument; formal verification of switcher 'underway ... early stages'
assumptions: loader hands ASR only to switcher
source: Chisnall-26, 3.2 Changing trust domain with the switcher, approx line 697
map_note: G-CF — switcher privilege uniqueness

statement: 'The switcher holds the only permit-unseal capability for the type used to seal trusted stacks.' Trusted stacks are set up by the loader and handed to the scheduler only as sealed capabilities.
assumptions: loader correctness
map_note: G-CF — trusted-stack confidentiality/integrity against the scheduler (RP5 is the mechanism)

statement: Switcher fail-stop: 'If the scheduler returns an invalid capability (one not sealed with the correct type) then the switcher will raise a fault.' 'If the exception program counter capability on exception entry is within the switcher's capability, the switcher will terminate. The switcher is written to avoid trapping and so any trap is assumed to be an active attack trying to exploit a bug in the switcher.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-CF — switcher self-protection: no re-entrant exception handling inside the switcher

statement: Cross-compartment call path obligations of the switcher: 'unsealing the capability that refers to the export table of the callee, clearing unused argument registers, pushing the information about the return to the trusted stack, subsetting the bounds of the stack, and zeroing the part of the stack passed to the callee. On return, it zeroes the stack again, zeroes unused return registers, and restores the callee's state.'
artifact: hand argument (export-table metadata gives register count, 6.2 approx line 2267)
assumptions: export table is loader-provisioned and sealed
map_note: G-c — the operational definition of the compartment-transition contract

statement: 'the switcher is the only component that has access to either two threads', or two compartments', state at the same time. As such, it is in the TCB for both compartment and thread isolation.' Mitigations: small ('similar number of instructions compared to the amount of unverified code in seL4'); defensive ('Most errors simply forcibly unwind to the previous trusted stack frame, so a compartment that attempts to attack the switcher exits to its caller'); 'it must follow the capability rules ... it is not able to access beyond the bounds of capabilities passed to it'; 'largely stateless. All state that it modifies is held in the trusted stack for the current thread.'
artifact: hand argument; formal verification in progress
assumptions: switcher is <500 instructions and 'expected to be amenable to formal verification'
map_note: G-CF — defines the switcher TCB and the properties AIVHAI's switcher-equivalent proof must discharge (no privilege opt-out, statelessness, unwind-on-error)

statement: 'trusted_stack_has_space(n) Returns true if the trusted stack contains at least requiredFrames frames past the current one, false otherwise.' A trusted stack frame is 'three capabilities (24 bytes)'; trusted_stack_frames 'defines the maximum cross-compartment call depth (including the entry point) for this thread.'
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 3.2 approx line 727; 4.5 approx line 1189; 8.1 approx line 3375
map_note: G-CF — bounded trusted-stack depth is a resource invariant of the switcher

statement: Scheduler trust scope: 'The scheduler is, by definition, in the TCB for availability ... It is not, however, in the TCB for confidentiality or integrity. The scheduler has no mechanism to inspect the state of an interrupted thread. When invoked explicitly, it is called with a normal cross-compartment call and so has no access to anything other than the arguments.' 'It doesn't run with elevated privileges ... it is not able to see the stacks or register states associated with threads.'
assumptions: register save area is on the trusted stack, which the scheduler sees only sealed (C26-034)
source: Chisnall-26, 3.3 Time slicing with the scheduler, approx lines 757-759; 8 intro approx line 3351
map_note: G-CF and G-c — scheduler excluded from confidentiality/integrity TCB; availability only

statement: 'Futexes are the only mechanism that the scheduler provides for blocking. Interrupts are mapped to futexes and so threads wait for hardware or software events in exactly the same way.' (Restated in 11.5: 'futexes are the only event source that can block'.)
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-CF — narrow scheduler interface (single blocking primitive) as an attack-surface invariant

statement: Allocator trust scope: 'trusted for confidentiality and integrity of memory allocated from the heap. If it incorrectly sets bounds, a compartment may gain access to memory belonging to another allocation. If it incorrectly configures revocation state or reuses memory too early then a use-after-free bug may become exploitable.' But 'The allocator is not able to bypass capability permissions, it simply holds a capability that spans the whole of heap memory ... It cannot access globals (or code) held in other compartments so a compartment that does not use the heap does not need to trust the allocator.'
assumptions: allocator has access to shadow bitmap and revoker (exclusive, see C26-124)
source: Chisnall-26, 3.4 Sharing memory from the allocator, approx lines 775-777
map_note: G-CF — allocator TCB scoped to the heap; it is not a general privilege holder

statement: 'calling a CHERI callback function will always be a cross-compartment call, even if the target is in the current compartment.' The address of a callback 'will be a sealed capability that can be used to invoke the compartment'; import-table entries are initialised by the loader 'with a sealed capability to the export table entry'.
assumptions: compiler correctness
map_note: G-c — cross-compartment function pointers are sealed, invocable only through the switcher (RP5 mechanism)

statement: Callback argument confinement: 'The callback is invoked in the compartment that implements it and has access to the copy of the counter (passed by value) that the caller provides, but it cannot modify the counter.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-c — by-value arguments do not leak authority

statement: Interrupt-state attribute rules: 'For cross-compartment calls, enabled is the default and inherit is not permitted. The compiler may not inline functions at call sites that would change the interrupt state and will always call them via a sentry capability set up by the loader. This makes it possible to statically reason about interrupt state in lexical scopes.' 'If a compartment is able to provide arbitrary interrupt-disabled functions, that compartment is in the TCB for availability.'
assumptions: compiler and loader correctness; auditing policy to restrict interrupt-disabled entry points
source: Chisnall-26, 5.4 Interrupt state control, approx lines 1493-1497
map_note: G-CF — availability TCB membership is auditable and structured

statement: Sealed opaque types: 'The hardware ensures that the caller cannot modify the underlying object. If the caller casts this to a char* and tries to modify it then they will get a run-time trap.' 'When a caller gives you back this kind of pointer and you unseal it, you will get a MyType* that is either a valid value or untagged.'
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 5.6 Sealing opaque types, approx lines 1601-1605
map_note: RP5 — software-visible consequence of sealed-capability opacity

statement: Guarded manipulation: 'You can't, for example, arbitrarily set the permissions on a capability, you can only remove permissions.' perms/and 'Clears all permissions except those provided as the argument'; tag/clear 'Invalidates the capability but preserves all other fields.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP3 — permissions never grow; and-permissions is the only permission-modifying operation

statement: Bounds-setting semantics: bounds/set 'Sets the base at or below the current address and the length at or above the requested length, as closely as possible to give a valid capability'; bounds/set_exact 'Sets the base to the current address and the length to the requested length or returns an untagged capability (one that will trap if used) if the result is not representable.'
assumptions: rounding is outward (toward wider bounds) but never beyond the source capability — the book does not say the latter explicitly here; it is implied by C26-004/C26-107
map_note: RP2 — this is the bounds-setting-rounding clause of RP2; note the source states rounding direction but not the containment-in-parent clause explicitly

statement: 'These two conditions ensure that stack pointers (which lack global) can be stored only on the stack (the only memory that has store-local permission).' (Heap allocation has global; stack allocation lacks global, has store-local.)
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-c — concrete confirmation of C26-008

statement: Permissions and bounds attach to the pointer, not the object: 'We have not removed permissions from an object, we have created a pointer that has fewer permissions to that object. There is no limit to the number of pointers that can exist to a single object.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP3 — derived capabilities are independent restrictions; no object-side state

statement: Exact equality 'returns true if the two capabilities ... are identical ... address, bounds, permissions, object type, and tag are all identical. It is, effectively, a bitwise comparison of all of the bits ... including the tag bits.' An untagged value 'is not a capability at all, merely 64 bits of data'.
assumptions: none stated
map_note: none — introspection semantics; useful as a definitional anchor for 'capability equality' in a Sail/Rocq spec

statement: Subset test: 'A capability is a subset of another if every right that it conveys is held by the other. This means the bounds of the subset capability must be smaller than or equal to the superset and all permissions held by the subset must be held by the superset.' An untagged capability is not a subset of anything ('no provenance guarantees').
assumptions: 'the test is most useful for telling if one capability is derived from another (or, at least, could have a derivation path from a specific common root)'
map_note: RP1 — the subset relation is the order with respect to which monotonicity is stated

statement: 'The temporal-safety properties of CHERIoT ensure that any dangling pointer to a heap object will be untagged and so any valid (tagged) pointer that is a subset of a heap allocation must be derived from the return from the original call to malloc or some similar function.'
assumptions: allocator correctness; revoker configured over all capability-bearing memory
map_note: RP1 and G-CF — provenance of live heap pointers; what the claims mechanism relies on

statement: Compressed bounds representability: 'The current CHERIoT encoding gives byte-granularity bounds for objects up to 511 bytes, then requires one more bit of alignment for each bit needed to represent the size, up to 8 MiB. Capabilities larger than 8 MiB must be aligned on an 8 MiB boundary for their base and top.' Nine-bit mantissa, shared exponent.
assumptions: CHERIoT 32-bit-address encoding; 'Future versions of CHERIoT are likely to support slightly more expressive formats'
source: Chisnall-26, 5.9 Sizing allocations, approx lines 1866-1872; 2.3 approx line 424
map_note: RP2 — the representability constraint that RP2's rounding clause must respect; will differ for the 64-bit RVY encoding

statement: '__builtin_cheri_round_representable_length returns the smallest length that is larger than (or equal to) the requested length and can be accurately represented'; representable_alignment_mask gives the mask 'applied to the base and top addresses to align them'. 'The allocator is using these internally'.
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP2 — rounding is upward-only and allocator-visible

statement: Sub-object bounds are not a guarantee: 'The compiler does not ensure that there is no way for actively malicious code within the same compartment to find a pointer with wider bounds. The heuristics that the compiler uses to decide where to apply bounds may also change over time.'
assumptions: intra-compartment only
source: Chisnall-26, 5.11 Enforcing sub-object bounds, approx line 2045
map_note: none — explicit non-claim; intra-compartment spatial safety is not part of G-c

statement: 'In CHERIoT, compartments and libraries can export only functions as entry points. Global variables are always private to a compartment or library, unless a pointer is explicitly passed out as a function argument or return in a cross-compartment call.'
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 6.1 Compartments and libraries export functions, approx line 2143
map_note: G-c — no ambient global sharing

statement: Read-only broadcast: 'Returning a read-only pointer to a global ... The owning compartment can write to the global and other compartments can read from their copy of the pointer, with guarantees that only the owning compartment is making changes.'
assumptions: owner strips store (and load-mutable for deep) before delegating
map_note: RP3 applied to G-c — single-writer invariant from permission narrowing

statement: Compartment structure: 'The core of a compartment is made of just two capabilities. The program counter capability (PCC) defines (and grants access to) the range of memory covering the compartment's code and read-only globals. This has read and execute permissions. The capability global pointer (CGP) defines (and grants access to) the range of memory covering the compartment's mutable globals.' Observed: PCC regions of distinct compartments 'do not overlap'; CGP differs per compartment.
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 6.2 Understanding the structure of a compartment, approx lines 2211-2238
map_note: G-c — definition of the compartment's ambient authority

statement: 'The read-only data region contains an import table. This is the only region of memory that, at system start, is allowed to contain capabilities that grant access outside of the PCC and CGP region for the compartment. The instructions for the loader to populate these are in the firmware image and are amenable to auditing.'
assumptions: initial state only
map_note: G-c — all initial cross-boundary authority is enumerable (import table)

statement: Export table contents define the switcher's transition: 'the PCC and CGP for the compartment and ... for each exported function: The location of the entry point; Whether interrupts are enabled or disabled when invoking this function; How many argument registers are used (conversely, how many are unused and should be zeroed). This is all of the information that the switcher needs to transition from one compartment to another.'
assumptions: export table is reachable only via loader-sealed capability
map_note: G-c — the data the switcher trusts; its integrity (sealed) is RP5

statement: Core-component trust model: 'the scheduler is written as a safebox ... assumes that everything else is trying to make it crash. The memory allocator is also written as a safebox, assuming that everything else is trying to either make it crash or leak powerful capabilities.' 'everything in the CHERIoT system trusts the scheduler for availability. Most things trust the allocator to enforce spatial and temporal memory safety for the heap.'
assumptions: 'It does not, for example, try to check that the memory allocator is returning disjoint capabilities' — scheduler trusts allocator for heap safety
source: Chisnall-26, 6.4 Choosing a trust model, approx line 2355
map_note: G-CF — states the trust relations between firmware components that a CF proof must either discharge or assume

statement: Safebox claim: 'Try modifying only runner.cc in this example to leak the secret without any incorrect guesses. Hopefully, you will find it impossible.' (A compartment holding a secret cannot have it read by a caller compartment.)
assumptions: 'Hopefully' — stated as challenge, not proof
source: Chisnall-26, 6.5 Implementing a safebox, approx line 2393
map_note: G-c — confidentiality of compartment-private state

statement: token_key_new: 'guaranteed to complete unless the allocator has exhausted the total number of sealing keys possible (2^32 - 2^24). After this point, it will never succeed.' 'There is no mechanism to reuse sealing capabilities.' 'This API is guaranteed never to block.' Returned key has permit-seal and permit-unseal; 'Callers may remove one or both'.
assumptions: 'A compartment that is granted access to this entry point is trusted not to exhaust this resource' (a 20 MHz core could exhaust it 'in around a day')
source: Chisnall-26, 6.6 Building software capabilities with sealing, approx lines 2401-2417
map_note: G-CF — allocator resource invariant (monotone key allocation, no reuse) with an explicit availability caveat

statement: Static sealed objects: 'The object created with this macro can be accessed only by code that has access to the sealing key.' Macros name both key and compartment so 'accidental name collisions don't lead to security vulnerabilities'; using an unexported sealing type 'will result in a linker error'.
assumptions: loader seals with the correct key
map_note: RP5 applied to G-c — software-defined capabilities are unforgeable handles

statement: 'This shows how sealing enforces type safety even in the presence of untrusted code.' Unsealed value of the right type fails unseal; sealed value of the wrong type fails unseal; direct access to the sealed object traps (SealViolation) and invokes the error handler.
assumptions: none stated
map_note: RP5 — type confinement via sealing, exercised end-to-end

statement: 'A compartment can allocate memory only if it has an allocation capability and any allocation capability that it holds shows up in the audit report when linking a firmware image.' 'The full contents of any object created in this way shows up in the audit log.'
assumptions: policy must check contents are well-formed (quota word + 20 zero bytes)
map_note: G-CF — heap authority is enumerable at link time

statement: Software permission bits: token-sealed capabilities 'are all at least 8-byte aligned (and, because they point to the start of the header, 8 bytes added to the base is always in bounds)'; the low three address bits carry user permissions; token_permissions_and 'mirrors the and-permissions operation supported by CHERI capabilities' and 'the permissions are on the sealed pointer, not the unsealed version.'
assumptions: token library implements and-only semantics
source: Chisnall-26, 6.7 Using permissions on software-defined capabilities, approx lines 2585-2649
map_note: RP3 lifted to software capabilities — monotone permission narrowing on sealed handles

statement: Pre-shared objects: 'Each import can have a different set of permissions' (load, store, load/store caps, load-mutable; 'load-mutable depends on both load and load/store capability permissions'). 'The type cannot be enforced by CHERI and depends on the compartment that imports the object. If a single compartment has write access to an object then that compartment forms the TCB for type safety of that object.'
assumptions: type safety of shared objects is a software TCB matter, not hardware
source: Chisnall-26, 6.8 Sharing globals between compartments, approx lines 2743-2775
map_note: G-c — shared-memory channels are per-import permission-restricted; explicit non-claim on type safety

statement: Availability invariant: 'Threads are scheduled independently and provide a building block for availability guarantees. Only a higher-priority thread or code running with interrupts disabled can prevent an unrelated thread from making progress.'
assumptions: scheduler correctness; interrupt-disabled code is bounded (C26-022)
map_note: G-CF — availability; note AIVHAI treats availability as a distinct, harder claim (SL-AIVHAI-P04), and this is the book's only crisp availability statement

statement: check_pointer contract: 'Checks that ptr is valid, unsealed, has at least Permissions, and has at least space bytes after the current offset. If the permissions do not include Global, then this will also check that the capability does not point to the current thread's stack.' Purpose: a caller may pass pointers lacking write/read/global, too short, invalid, or overlapping the callee's stack; check_pointer 'prevents information disclosure by ensuring that the string does not overlap the current compartment invocation's stack'.
assumptions: 'In general, a pointer cannot be modified after it's been checked, but the memory that a pointer refers to may be freed' — TOCTOU on heap requires claims
source: Chisnall-26, 6.10 Validating arguments, approx lines 2827-2869; 6.15 approx line 3095
map_note: G-c — defensive validation at the compartment boundary; the stack-overlap check is a consequence of C26-023 (callee's stack is a subset of the thread stack)

statement: heap_address_is_valid: 'If this returns false but the pointer has global permission, it must be a global and so does not need to be claimed. If the pointer lacks global permission then it cannot be claimed, but if this function returns false then it is guaranteed not to go away for the duration of the call.'
assumptions: memory partitioning: heap vs. globals vs. stacks (14.1)
map_note: G-c — lifetime classification of pointers by permission + address range

statement: Stack-space check: 'Before entering a compartment, the switcher will check the amount of stack space against the required amount in the export table.' With __cheriot_minimum_stack, 'the switcher will not invoke the exported function unless at least the required amount of stack space is available' (caller gets -ENOTENOUGHSTACK). 'The switcher check is not intended to ensure that the invocation of the current compartment can succeed, only that failures are detectable and recoverable.'
assumptions: compiler fills the default from the leaf entry function only
source: Chisnall-26, 6.11 Ensuring adequate stack space, approx lines 2939-2957
map_note: G-CF — switcher-enforced precondition on entry; scoped as detectability, not liveness

statement: 'CHERIoT CPUs include a feature called a stack high-water mark that tracks the amount of stack that is used so that the switcher can avoid zeroing unused portions of the stack.' stack_lowest_used_address 'Returns the lowest address that has been stored to on the stack in this compartment invocation.'
assumptions: correctness of zeroing-elision depends on the high-water-mark CSR being sound (every store below the mark is tracked)
map_note: G-c — the soundness of C26-023's stack zeroing depends on this microarchitectural tracker; a hardware obligation AIVHAI's RTL proof could discharge

statement: Fault routing: 'Asynchronous interrupts are all routed to the scheduler ... Synchronous faults are (optionally) delivered to the compartment that caused them.' The switcher looks first for a rich handler, then a stackless one; 'If not implemented then compartment faults will unwind the trusted stack.' On forced unwind 'the return registers will be set to -1' (-ECOMPARTMENTFAIL).
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 6.12 Handling errors approx lines 2977-2995; 6.13 approx line 3005; 6.15 approx line 3087
map_note: G-c — faults never escape the faulting compartment except as an unwind to its caller

statement: Error-handler confidentiality: 'The spilled register file does not contain a tagged value for the program counter capability. This is to prevent library functions that run with interrupts disabled or with access to secrets from accidentally leaking on faults. All other registers will be preserved exactly as they are in the register file.' On resume the switcher rederives 'the PCC from the compartment's code capability'.
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 6.13 Writing rich error handlers, approx lines 3023-3027
map_note: G-CF and RP5 — a handler cannot obtain an executable capability to code it was not already authorised for

statement: 'The error handler is called with interrupts enabled, even if interrupts were disabled in the faulting code. Latency-critical code should never depend on the error handler for meeting its timing.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-CF — availability: a fault cannot extend an interrupt-disabled region

statement: Handler reentrancy guarantee: 'if a call to heap_allocate fails then that error will be handled in the allocator compartment. Your error handler will never be invoked in the middle of a call to the allocator and so it is fine to use error handlers to release locks and free memory.'
assumptions: faults are per-compartment (C26-074)
map_note: G-c — fault isolation gives per-compartment handler atomicity

statement: Static threads and the no-capture argument: 'Threads in CHERIoT RTOS cannot be dynamically created ... The no-capture guarantees that CHERIoT RTOS enforces are based on the guarantee that no code other than the loader has access to two stacks' memory at a time and so the switcher can zero stacks and avoid leaks. The only store-local capabilities that a thread ever has access to are derived from its current stack.' 'The security model requires a static guarantee that no memory moves between being stack memory ... and non-stack (global or heap) memory. The trusted stack memory and save area memory should never be visible outside of the switcher. Without these static properties, the allocator would be in the TCB for thread and compartment isolation.'
assumptions: static thread table; thread exit 'does not free the thread's stack or trusted stack'
source: Chisnall-26, 8.1 Defining threads approx lines 3355-3357; 16.2 approx lines 6726-6732
map_note: G-c and G-CF — the invariant set that keeps the allocator out of the isolation TCB; load-bearing for AIVHAI's 64-bit microkernel extension where stacks/threads may be dynamic

statement: 'the stack-pointer capability will be bounded to this size (rounded up if necessary for alignment) and any overflow of the stack, even by a single byte, will trap. The trusted stack size is the maximum number of cross-compartment calls that this thread can do.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-c — stack bounds are hardware-enforced per thread; follows from RP2 given loader provisioning

statement: Realtime scoping: 'A thread may block for more than the permitted limit if it is sleeping while a higher-priority thread runs. Only the highest-priority thread can make strong realtime guarantees in the presence of other runnable threads.' thread_sleep: 'The thread becomes runnable once the timeout has expired but a higher-priority thread may prevent it from actually being scheduled.'
assumptions: priority scheduler; tickless
map_note: G-CF — explicit scope limit on availability guarantees

statement: 'Timeout structures may not be stored on the heap. Any function checking timeouts may refuse to accept a heap-allocated timeout' (deallocation while sleeping would crash the sleeper).
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 8.3 Limiting blocking with timeouts, approx line 3469
map_note: G-CF — scheduler self-protection against caller-controlled deallocation

statement: futex_wake least privilege: 'the scheduler does not require any explicit permissions. The scheduler never needs store access to the futex word. Removing store permission means that a compromised scheduler can cause spurious wakes but cannot tamper with the futex word. If, for example, the futex word is a lock then the scheduler can wake threads that are blocked on the lock but cannot release the lock and so cannot make two threads believe that they have simultaneously acquired the same lock.'
assumptions: callers pass read-only futex pointers
source: Chisnall-26, 8.5 Waiting for events with futexes, approx line 3615
map_note: G-CF — scheduler is excluded from lock-integrity TCB; a concrete instance of RP3 limiting a privileged component

statement: 'The futex APIs are designed to allow this combination of wait and atomic operation to work for any interleaving.' (futex_timed_wait compares to expected and sleeps only on match.)
assumptions: single-core; atomics via interrupt-disabled helpers
map_note: G-CF — scheduler liveness/correctness of the single blocking primitive

statement: Priority inheritance: 'The specified thread will have its priority set to the highest priority of any of the waiting threads. The priority boost lasts until the waiters time out or the boosted thread releases the lock, whichever happens first. A single thread can hold multiple priority-inheriting locks and receive priority boosts from all of them.'
assumptions: owner thread ID stored in low 16 bits of futex word by the lock implementation
map_note: G-CF — availability mechanism; not part of AIVHAI's formal boundary

statement: Futex sharing limit: 'if a flag lock is directly accessible by two mutually distrusting compartments, one can write an invalid value to the word and either prevent the other from waking waiters or cause it to spuriously believe that it has acquired the lock.' 'There is one situation where futexes are safe to share across compartment boundaries. If you have a component that others trust for availability, it can share read-only views of a futex to allow waiting for an out-of-band event. The scheduler does this for interrupts.'
assumptions: none stated
map_note: G-c — explicit non-claim: lock integrity across distrust is not provided; read-only futex delegation is

statement: Sealed message queues: 'Nowhere outside of the queue compartment can unseal this so the queue is protected against tampering. The queue may still contain malicious or malformed data, but you have guarantees that messages will arrive in order and that they won't be tampered with in flight.' Restricted handles: 'neither compartment that holds a send or receive handle can free the queue, nor can they be used for the opposite operation, and the queue compartment protects the integrity of the queue itself.'
assumptions: queue compartment correctness; library (unsealed) queues 'are not intended to be robust in the presence of malicious callers'
source: Chisnall-26, 8.11 Sending messages between compartments, approx lines 4061-4067, 4185; 8.10 approx line 3977
map_note: G-c — integrity of an RTOS IPC channel derived from RP5 and allocator ownership

statement: 'You cannot free an object pointed to by a sealed capability unless you also have the capability that authorises unsealing ... Similarly, you cannot free a sealed object unless you hold the allocation capability that allocated it.' token-allocated objects 'can be deallocated only by presenting both the allocator capability and the sealing capability that match the original allocation.'
assumptions: allocator correctness
map_note: G-CF — allocator ownership/lifetime invariant

statement: Heap bounds monotonicity: 'Every pointer to a new allocation provided by the memory allocator is derived from a capability to a large heap region and bounded. The capability monotonicity guarantees in a CHERI system ensure that a caller cannot expand the bounds of the returned pointer.'
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 9.3 Recalling the memory safety guarantees, approx line 4331
map_note: RP2 — the book's explicit 'bounds never widen' statement, named 'capability monotonicity'

statement: Load filter: 'When a capability is loaded from memory into a register, the load filter checks the revocation bit associated with the base of the capability and clears the tag bit if the capability points to freed memory ... The load filter ensures that you cannot load, and therefore cannot try to use, any dangling pointers. This gives deterministic use-after-free protection; any attempt to use a pointer to a deallocated object will trap.'
artifact: Sail model (load filter is in the CHERIoT core); shadow bitmap MMIO
assumptions: revocation bitmap (one bit per 8 bytes of heap) correctly painted by the allocator; heap memory must be in the load-filter range (14.1)
map_note: RP4-adjacent and G-CF — hardware clears tags on load of revoked capabilities; a tag-clearing (never tag-setting) operation, so consistent with RP1/RP4

statement: Revoker and base invariant: 'The revoker periodically scans all memory and invalidates any pointers whose base address points to a deallocated object. The monotonicity of bounds ensures that the base of a capability always points either somewhere within the allocation or, if the length is zero, to the word immediately after it.' 'The allocator marks the metadata between allocations as freed. This means that a zero-length capability to the end of an object is likely to be untagged.'
assumptions: revoker scans globals, stacks and heap (14.1 line ~6516); heap_free footnote: a tagged zero-length past-the-end capability 'will result in -EINVAL'
map_note: RP2 — a corollary of bounds monotonicity used to make base-keyed revocation sound

statement: Asynchronous sweep soundness: 'The load filter ensures that no new pointers to deallocated objects can appear in memory so the revocation sweep can proceed asynchronously. Any object that is in quarantine at the start of a sweep is safe to remove from quarantine at the end.' 'This combination of features allows the allocator to provide complete spatial and temporal safety for heap objects.'
assumptions: load filter + revoker both present ('hardware' revoker expected on all real implementations; 'software' revoker for Sail; none for benchmarking only, 14.4)
map_note: G-CF — the allocator's temporal-safety argument; the 'complete ... temporal safety' claim is the strongest allocator claim in the book

statement: heap_free semantics: 'we actually free / release the allocation associated with the base of ptr, not the address. This is because the base is guaranteed to be within the bounds of the original allocation due to capability monotonicity, unlike the address (which is ignored).' Freeing requires 'a capability to the entire allocation with the same bounds as returned by heap_allocate'; claims may be released with reduced bounds.
assumptions: none stated
source: Chisnall-26, 9.4 Allocating with an explicit capability, approx line 4389
map_note: RP2 applied in G-CF — allocator relies on bounds monotonicity for its free-path correctness
