assumptions: Baremetal RVY firmware on the Sail model; red-team demo; unauthorised accesses expected to fault
map_note: G-CF4: PCC bounded at entry

statement: Demo protection ASR: access-system-registers permission is removed from the compartment (weakened variant retains it).
assumptions: As above
map_note: G-CF4: no ASR

statement: Demo protection DDC: the Default Data Capability is cleared on entry (weakened variant leaves an unbounded DDC in place).
assumptions: As above
map_note: G-CF4: no DDC

statement: Demo protection REGS_TEMP: registers and associated CSR contents are scrubbed at entry (weakened variant skips the scrub, leaving residual contents available).
assumptions: As above
map_note: G-CF4: registers scrubbed

statement: Attack scope: attacks are permitted only from code inside the supplied blob after execution reaches compartment_enter; a successful attack reads, modifies, or obtains capability authority over assets outside the compartment (write_var, read_var, cheri_infinite_cap, other external memory and capabilities); availability and other attacks are out of scope.
assumptions: Bootstrap code and all execution before compartment_enter, and the trusted handlers in fw_compartment.S, are outside the attack scope; return and trap paths may be exercised
map_note: G-CF: the demo's success criterion is a violation of G-CF; the exclusion of bootstrap is the A-5 trust assumption

statement: The compartment is jumped to in capability mode; payloads not built in purecap mode will likely trigger faults within the first few instructions.
assumptions: Raw binary, entry at byte offset zero
map_note: G-CF4: entry in capability mode

statement: A capability tag attests derivation by a permitted sequence of rights-non-increasing operations; invalid operations clear the tag; using an invalid or out-of-bounds capability traps before the operation is performed.
assumptions: ISA-level property restated by the OS paper
map_note: G-CF: hardware basis for every isolation claim

statement: CHERIoT has no MMU or MPU; CHERI is the only isolation mechanism present.
assumptions: Low-cost real-time targets
map_note: G-CF: isolation rests entirely on capability enforcement

statement: Load filter: whenever a capability is loaded from memory the CPU checks the revocation bit for the capability's base and, if set, clears the tag; because bounds can only shrink, the base is always within the original allocation.
assumptions: Per-granule revocation bits in separate SRAM
map_note: GAP-9: hardware primitive for reuse-after-free safety

statement: The revoker scans every capability in memory in parallel with execution; once all memory has been swept no valid capabilities exist to any object freed before the sweep, and the memory can be reused.
assumptions: Full sweep of 1 MiB at 250 MHz is about 1.5 ms
map_note: GAP-9: reuse is gated on a complete sweep

statement: Shallow no-capture: a capability lacking the global permission may be stored only through a permit-store-local capability (stacks and register-save areas only), so an untrusted callee cannot keep a non-global argument after returning, though it may keep a global capability loaded through it.
assumptions: Only stacks and register-save areas carry permit-store-local
map_note: GAP-4: the mechanism for call-scoped delegation

statement: Deep immutability: any capability loaded through a capability lacking permit-load-mutable has permit-store and permit-load-mutable removed, so a bad callee cannot modify anything reachable from the argument.
assumptions: CHERIoT-specific permission
map_note: GAP-4: deep read-only delegation

statement: Deep no-capture: any capability loaded through a capability lacking permit-load-global has global and permit-load-global removed, so a callee cannot capture anything reachable from the argument.
assumptions: CHERIoT-specific permission
map_note: GAP-4: deep call-scoped delegation

statement: Sentries grant access to a function without exposing PC-relative data; return addresses are sealed as backward sentries so the callee can jump back only to that address; forward sentries carry interrupt posture, and non-TCB software cannot directly enable or disable interrupts.
assumptions: Structured programming model on interrupt posture
map_note: G-CF4 for the return path; GAP-1 for interrupt posture

statement: Threat model: the TCB (loader, switcher, allocator, scheduler) is assumed bug-free and not backdoored; no correctness is assumed of compilers for untrusted components; an attacker may run arbitrary instructions in a compartment; hardware is assumed free of bugs and side channels; physical attacks are out of scope.
assumptions: Cites CHERI ISA formal verification and ongoing CHERIoT hardware and software verification
map_note: G-CF: adversary and TCB assumptions

statement: Threads can access only their current compartment's code and data, the call's arguments, a subset of their stack exclusive to the call, and transitively reachable resources.
assumptions: Hybrid model: compartments isolate at code boundaries, threads isolate flows
map_note: G-CF: per-thread reachable set

statement: Threads may exchange capabilities and data through shared memory but are otherwise isolated from one another (flow isolation); multiple threads may share a compartment under preemptive scheduling.
assumptions: One core; preemptive scheduling
map_note: GAP-1: shared compartments under preemption are in CHERIoT's model, not AIVHAI's

statement: Shared libraries execute in the caller's security domain and must have no mutable globals, so they cannot transfer or leak state between calling compartments and threads.
assumptions: Read-only data must be reached via explicit functions
map_note: G-CF: shared code cannot become a covert channel

statement: Aside from the loader (fully trusted, boot only), no runtime component, even in the TCB, runs with all privileges; each TCB compartment is trusted to enforce a specific property whose failure would be insufficient by itself to take complete control.
assumptions: Figure 2 trust decomposition
map_note: G-CF: firmware's own state is not reachable from any single component

statement: The loader's only input is the firmware image; it refines the omnipotent root set deterministically, runs only during boot, and is erased before control passes to the scheduler; after it exits nothing in the system is omnipotent.
assumptions: Memory after loader can be dumped for arbitrary verification
source: AmarChenChisnallEtAl-25.md L153, L163; cheriot-rtos/docs/architecture.md L46-48; faq.md L42-48
map_note: A-5: root authority does not survive bootstrap

statement: At boot, only the import table of a compartment may contain pointers that authorise access to memory not owned by that compartment (MMIO, sentries, sealed export-table capabilities, sealed static objects); the export table is accessible only to the switcher.
assumptions: Basis of the linker audit report
map_note: A-5 and G-CF: the post-bootstrap capability graph is enumerable

statement: The switcher is the most privileged runtime component (~355 instructions); a malicious switcher can compromise availability and partially confidentiality and integrity via thread register files and stacks, but cannot directly access any other memory.
assumptions: FAQ: compromise 'almost certainly provides sufficient primitives' to eventually gain full control
map_note: G-CF: residual trust in the switcher

statement: Each thread's trusted stack is accessible exclusively to the switcher after boot; only the switcher holds a PCC with the special permission granting access to the control register holding the trusted-stack capability (mtdc, via access-system-registers).
assumptions: Switcher runs mostly with interrupts disabled
map_note: G-CF4: ASR confined to the switcher

statement: Only the switcher holds the capability that unseals import-table references to export tables, as the sole entity trusted to perform domain switches.
assumptions: Sealed capability base points at the callee export table
map_note: G-CF4: entry only through the switcher

statement: On a compartment call the switcher pushes a trusted-stack frame, clears all non-argument registers, truncates the stack capability, zeroes the new stack memory and jumps; on return it zeroes the stack, restores the caller's code, data and stack capabilities, and zeroes all non-return registers.
assumptions: Cost measured at 209 cycles empty call
map_note: G-CF4: registers scrubbed and stack bounded at entry and return

statement: Each cross-compartment call shrinks the stack so that all state created by existing compartments is inaccessible to the new callee.
assumptions: Single stack per thread
map_note: G-CF4: caller frames unreachable from callee

statement: The allocator is trusted for heap memory safety only; it has access only to heap memory, and a bug in it cannot violate memory safety for compartment globals or stack allocations.
assumptions: 3.1K LoC, 16 entry points
map_note: GAP-9: heap lifetime is the allocator's responsibility

statement: Accesses to freed objects trap as soon as free returns, not only after the revocation pass; the allocator alone may access freed memory through a privileged capability whose loads do not consult revocation bits.
assumptions: Contrast with Cornucopia's UAF/UAR gap
map_note: GAP-9: no use-after-free window

statement: Freed memory is quarantined until a full revocation sweep has completed; the allocator drains a small constant number of quarantined objects per malloc/free.
assumptions: Hardware-exposed sweep counter
map_note: GAP-9: reuse gated on sweep completion

statement: The whole heap is zeroed at boot and objects are erased in free(); the allocator's exclusive access to freed memory ensures the zeros persist to reuse; heap_allocate memory is guaranteed zeroed.
assumptions: Uninitialized leaks remain possible only with custom memory management or non-zeroed stack buffers
map_note: GAP-9: no residue across reuse

statement: The scheduler is trusted for availability only; it cannot unseal the stacks and registers of interrupted threads, its outputs are checked by the switcher, and it sees only explicitly passed arguments.
assumptions: Scheduler is a normal compartment apart from its switcher entry point
source: AmarChenChisnallEtAl-25.md L195; cheriot-rtos/docs/faq.md L54-57; architecture.md L70
map_note: GAP-1: preemption without a confidentiality-trusted scheduler

statement: Opaque objects: sealed capabilities can be exported and re-imported with assurance the object was not tampered with; the token API virtualises sealing because the hardware offers only seven object types.
assumptions: Two compartments sharing a hardware sealing key could unseal each other's objects
map_note: GAP-4: software-defined delegated references

statement: Allocation capabilities carry quotas; only holders may allocate; heap_free requires an allocation capability matching the one used to allocate.
assumptions: Quotas auditable from the firmware report
map_note: GAP-4: delegated allocation authority

statement: Quota delegation hazards: a caller allocating on the callee's behalf can free memory out from under the callee to trigger faults; the sealed allocation API (requiring both allocation capability and virtual sealing type) prevents this; deep no-capture prevents the callee from retaining the allocation capability.
assumptions: Endpoints without global state can only DoS the caller itself
map_note: GAP-4: runtime delegation of allocation authority and its revocation

statement: Futex-based locks: the scheduler can spuriously wake or fail to wake a thread (availability) but cannot modify the lock word to make two threads believe they hold the same lock (integrity).
assumptions: Scheduler holds only a load capability to the futex word, not retained
map_note: GAP-1: synchronisation under preemption

statement: Interface hardening: before sharing a capability compartments should tighten bounds and permissions (read-only, deeply immutable, non-capturable); inputs crossing trust domains must be checked for tag, length, permissions and sealing.
assumptions: Correct use is the integrator's responsibility
map_note: GAP-4: de-privileging at the delegation point

statement: Temporal TOCTOU: a bad compartment can free an object another is using; claims (quota-charged) and ephemeral claims (until next compartment call, hazard-pointer style in the switcher) prevent the allocator from freeing it.
assumptions: Core compartments otherwise avoid this by running with interrupts disabled
source: AmarChenChisnallEtAl-25.md L254; cheriot-rtos/docs/AllocatorClaims.md L162-176; Allocator.md L69-76
map_note: GAP-1 and GAP-9: concurrent free of shared objects

statement: Cross-compartment control-flow integrity: functions not exposed via an annotation cannot be called by any other compartment; entry points a compartment's code does not call are absent from its import table and thus not callable at run time.
assumptions: Compiler-populated import/export tables
map_note: G-CF4: entry restricted to declared points

statement: Entry points declare minimum stack space, protecting against a caller invoking an API with a small stack to trigger stack-overflow faults in the callee; allocator APIs refuse to run with insufficient stack (-ENOTENOUGHSTACK) because an attacker could otherwise trigger arbitrary failures in the allocator.
assumptions: Stack watermark tooling
map_note: G-CF4: caller-controlled stack depth as an attack on the callee

statement: Error handlers run in the compartment's context and rights; illegal operations trap before affecting data so the program is in a defined state; handlers may resume, unwind or micro-reboot; without a handler the switcher unwinds.
assumptions: Only synchronous faults
map_note: GAP-9: micro-reboot is the reset-and-reuse mechanism

statement: In the error handler the spilled PCC is stored untagged to prevent leaking secrets from shared libraries; shared libraries with secrets must not hold them in registers during operations that may trap.
assumptions: Resume re-derives PCC from the compartment's PCC
map_note: G-CF4: trap path does not leak code capabilities

statement: The error handler runs on the compartment's stack and cannot handle out-of-stack conditions; a compartment that runs out of stack unwinds unconditionally, so any caller-controlled value influencing callee stack depth can force an unwind without cleanup.
assumptions: Callee may clean up on next entry if tracked in globals
map_note: G-CF4: boundary invariant on stack is not enough to protect callee state

statement: On any forced unwind the return registers are set to -1 and 0; compartments without an error handler cannot distinguish a callee returning -1 from a forced unwind.
assumptions: Advice: avoid returning -1 for success
map_note: none: return-value ambiguity on fault

statement: Micro-reboot: prevent new threads entering, rewind all threads in the compartment (switcher API), release all heap data by quota, reset globals from read-only snapshots; persistent state goes to a separate state-store compartment.
assumptions: Case study: TCP/IP stack micro-reboot in 0.27 s
map_note: GAP-9: concrete destruction-and-reuse procedure for a live compartment

statement: Assuming error-handling mechanisms are correctly used, memory-safety bugs cannot impact confidentiality, integrity, or availability.
assumptions: Red-team adversarial evaluation; 'no defense is perfect'
map_note: G-CF: claimed consequence for memory-safety faults

statement: Repeat attacks: a strong attacker can repeatedly trigger traps forcing a victim compartment to spend all its cycles micro-rebooting; this DoS is not prevented.
assumptions: Fundamental to micro-reboots; shadow compartments suggested
map_note: GAP-1: availability under repeated faults

statement: Bugs that do not cause a trap (high-level logic bugs) cannot be prevented, only contained; a buggy error handler can incorrectly reset state.
assumptions: Only formal verification could prevent such bugs
map_note: G-CF: containment, not correctness

statement: Interface attacks by a compromised compartment on its callers or callees cannot be entirely ruled out; hardening APIs and cross-compartment CFI raise the number of interfaces that must be breached.
assumptions: Defenses effective only if integrator-controlled parts (handlers, hardening, auditing) are correct
map_note: GAP-4: delegated data is the residual attack surface

statement: TCB components are currently the target of formal verification building on the ISA formal model (VeriCHERI RTL verification and CHERIoT-Ibex observational correctness are cited); CHERIoT hardware and software 'are currently being formally verified'.
assumptions: No software-TCB proof artifact is presented in the paper; the cited works verify hardware
source: AmarChenChisnallEtAl-25.md L101, L302, refs [21] L514, [78] L642
map_note: G-CF: aspiration, no compartment-level proof in evidence

statement: By design no compartment can run code in the context of the loader; a backdoored library cannot access another compartment's memory at run time, and its new dependencies appear in the auditable firmware report.
assumptions: liblzma case study; no dynamic linking
map_note: A-5: supply-chain code cannot reacquire boot authority

statement: After the loader has run there are no memory regions to which both writeable and executable capabilities exist.
assumptions: May be relaxed for dynamic code generation
map_note: A-5: W^X holds from bootstrap

statement: Nothing outside a compartment can run its code except by calling a public entry point, and nothing outside can access its globals unless pointers to them are explicitly passed as arguments; code and globals therefore have confidentiality and integrity guarantees.
assumptions: Capability system, no ACLs
map_note: G-CF: direct statement of G-CF for CHERIoT

statement: Cross-compartment calls: only values explicitly passed as arguments are visible to the callee; only values explicitly returned propagate back; a non-global capability passed as argument may be used but not captured.
assumptions: Register and stack zeroing by the switcher
map_note: G-CF4 and GAP-4: what crosses the boundary

statement: Memory-safety threat model: a compartment is free to do whatever it wants with its own globals and portion of the stack (assembly may overwrite any of them except the caller's part of the stack) but must not violate memory safety for objects created in other compartments.
assumptions: Global and stack pointers are powerful sub-language capabilities
map_note: G-CF: intra-compartment safety is not claimed

statement: Use-after-free deterministically traps: loading a pointer to a deallocated object yields an untagged value, but this is not safe to test with interrupts enabled because an object can be freed during a context switch.
assumptions: Interrupt-disabled check required
map_note: GAP-1 and GAP-9: preemption interacts with reuse checks

statement: The software revocation loop (for i: current[i] = current[i], interrupts disabled) invalidates all dangling capabilities in the provided range as long as the hardware implements the correct read barrier check.
assumptions: 'Easy to audit'; correctness conditional on the load filter
map_note: GAP-9: software fallback for sweeping

statement: There is no notion of compartment or thread ID; it is a capability system, not an ACL system; an entity must actively choose to exercise a right, avoiding confused-deputy attacks; removing the global permission lets a right be delegated for the duration of a call so a service acting for C1 cannot invoke P with C2's rights.
assumptions: Principle of intentionality
map_note: GAP-4: delegation semantics that make per-call authority precise

statement: Static sealed objects are allocated outside any compartment's global region, accessed only via loader-provided capabilities, unsealable only with the authorising capability, and may not contain pointers.
assumptions: Visible to linker and auditable
map_note: A-5: build-time provisioned authority is loader-sealed

statement: Initialisers are invoked by the loader through the switcher on a one-deep trusted stack and the initialiser table must contain only cross-compartment calls.
assumptions: Proposal document for issue 275
map_note: A-5: bootstrap-time code reuses the isolated call path

statement: No user code runs directly from the interrupt handler; the scheduler runs it on a separate stack and maps interrupts to futex events; acknowledging an interrupt requires a capability, with wait and acknowledge permissions separated.
assumptions: Edge-triggered interrupts auto-completed
map_note: GAP-1 and GAP-4: interrupt authority is delegated, not ambient

statement: realloc is not provided because in-place resize is dangerous in a single-provenance pointer model: dangling capabilities with wider bounds would survive a shrink.
assumptions: Only allocate-copy-deallocate is safe
map_note: GAP-9: reuse of an object's own storage

statement: Simple reference counting is insufficient under mutual distrust: A allocates, passes to B, B increments, A decrements twice from another thread, B traps; each reference must be tracked per allocator ID.
assumptions: Claims consume the claimant's quota; sub-object claims unresolved
map_note: GAP-4 and GAP-9: delegated objects freed by a distrusting owner

statement: Threat model: untrusted dynamic libraries' ELF files are well-formed; the toolchain and dynamic linker are in the TCB; maliciously crafted ELF files are not addressed.
assumptions: Early prototype
map_note: G-CF: build-time trust

statement: The domain transition enforces well-bracketed control flow (authoritative return chain in a TCB-only trusted stack) and stack safety (distinct stack per compartment switched by the trampoline), citing Georges et al.'s formalisation.
assumptions: The formalisation cited is of an idealised capability machine, not this implementation
map_note: G-CF4: entry/return invariants

statement: The current prototype provides no security guarantees; register clearing is not done (caller-saved registers can leak), static-function pointers passed to another compartment execute with incorrect privileges, and interface vulnerabilities and shared buffers are not mitigated.
assumptions: 2023 workshop status
map_note: G-CF4 and GAP-4: gaps later addressed in the 2026 paper

statement: Threat model: kernel, dynamic linker, C/C++ runtime, threading library and a few privileged libc functions form the TCB; the compiler toolchain is trusted to produce well-formed ELF files that faithfully apply the policy; hardware is assumed to meet the CHERI ISA whose soundness has been formally verified; micro-architectural side channels and physical attacks are out of scope.
assumptions: Cites Bauereiss et al. (Morello) and Nienhuis et al. (CHERI-MIPS)
map_note: G-CF: trust boundary for c18n

statement: Monotonicity: no sequence of instructions can derive a capability that is not a subset of an existing capability; hence unforgeability: no valid capability can be created out of thin air.
assumptions: Proved for Morello and CHERI-MIPS ISA models by others; stated here as the primer
map_note: G-CF: the architectural ground for every containment claim
correction: Codex review of PR #246, Cycle 1: GaoBaldwinClarkeEtAl-26 reports the ISA proofs of others.

statement: Stack Safety: no compartment can access another compartment's stack frames except through explicitly shared capabilities; each thread uses a distinct stack per compartment switched by the trampoline; a callee receives a capability bounded to the spilled-argument area only.
assumptions: ABI change: variadic/spilled arguments passed via explicit bounded capability
map_note: G-CF4: caller frames unreachable at entry

statement: Register Integrity: callee-saved registers are saved in the protected trusted frame by the calling leg and restored by the returning leg, so a malicious callee cannot corrupt them.
assumptions: Trusted frames protected by Executive mode (Morello) or sealed UTIDC capability (RISC-V)
map_note: G-CF4: return-path register invariant

statement: Register Confidentiality: trampolines clear exactly the non-argument registers in the calling leg and non-return registers in the returning leg, using toolchain-emitted function signatures from both caller and callee; callers may declare more argument registers than the callee but not more return registers, so mismatched declarations cannot leak.
assumptions: Signatures can be incorrect in the presence of undefined behaviour
map_note: G-CF4: registers scrubbed both ways

statement: Control Flow Integrity: inter-compartment control flow is well-bracketed; all returning legs are interchangeable and rely solely on the Trusted Stack and Stack Lookup Table, so a callee cannot stash a return pointer, substitute another trampoline's returning leg, or return into a compartment under the wrong context; tail calls collapse trusted frames in place.
assumptions: Trampoline data header must never execute; relies on exposing only sentries to its entry and returning leg
map_note: G-CF4: return only to the recorded caller

statement: Mediation of transitions: inter-compartment references are obtained only through the GOT and wrapped in trampolines (the compiler never derives function pointers from PC), the kernel accepts system calls only from C-runtime wrappers carrying an unforgeable user-defined permission bit on PCC, and signals go first to a centralised handler that completes any interrupted TCB critical section.
assumptions: Wrapper symbols remain subject to the ACL
map_note: G-CF4: no bypass of the transition by pointer, trap, or signal

statement: Trusted compartments opt out of ABI hygiene; stateless libc functions (memcpy, strcmp) are placed in one by default; statelessness is neither sufficient nor necessary and such code must be audited not to corrupt caller state; mutually-trusting sets can be coalesced.
assumptions: Performance motivation
map_note: GAP-4: audited code runs without the boundary invariants

statement: Compartmentalization Policy Enforcement: the static linker rejects prohibited references and records ACL-derived permission constraints (e.g. read-only capability to a writable symbol), the dynamic linker bounds code capabilities to sub-library images with padding so rounded bounds do not overlap; stack, heap and JIT capabilities are constrained dynamically by CheriABI.
assumptions: Data-dependent sharing without knowing recipients at allocation
map_note: G-CF: link-time policy on code and globals

statement: Baseline CheriABI temporal safety: capabilities to freed or unmapped regions are revoked before storage or addresses are reused, even when delegated across compartments; unloading a shared library or retiring a JIT mapping revokes capabilities into that region.
assumptions: Cornucopia Reloaded enabled by default; disabled for the gRPC benchmark
map_note: GAP-9: cross-compartment reuse is revocation-gated

statement: Limitations: setjmp exposes the calling compartment's machine state; signal handlers receive the interrupted compartment's context; file descriptors are process-granular; dlopen, ptrace, dl_iterate_phdr, elf_aux_info grant wide authority; assembly-generated wild function pointers do not cause transitions; thread-local storage is not compartmentalised.
assumptions: Some called inherent, others engineering
map_note: G-CF and GAP-4: ambient-authority APIs breach isolation

statement: Stack references passed across compartment boundaries, including implicit argument buffers, can be hoarded beyond their lifetimes; stack temporal safety is deferred (CHERIoT's restriction on storing stack references is incompatible with the C standard).
assumptions: Shadow stacks partially mitigate
map_note: GAP-9: stack lifetime across delegation

statement: Interface safety: programmers remain responsible for compartment interface vulnerabilities arising from intentional sharing; speculative execution can leak compartment secrets.
assumptions: RLBox-style taint tracking and speculation contracts suggested
map_note: GAP-4: delegated data validation is out of scope

statement: CheriTree exact capability-graph traversal: all valid capabilities can be identified by tag and the reachable memory from a point of execution computed exhaustively; in tcpdump an unexpected jmp_buf made print-ether and the netdissect stack reachable until sealed into a sentry.
assumptions: Run-time snapshot, not a proof
map_note: G-CF: an auditing method for the reachable set; the AIVHAI optional audit is this

statement: c18n 'does not yet provide complete isolation between compartments': any compartment can access any other compartment's thread-local variables; dlopen can access privileged rtld data; longjmp and C++ exceptions can cross boundaries destroying other compartments' frames; signal handlers can inspect or modify another compartment's machine context.
assumptions: Shipping man page, May 2026
map_note: G-CF and G-CF4: documented isolation holes in the production prototype

statement: Compartment transition tracing and overhead simulation reduce security and are for debugging only.
assumptions: ktrace facility
map_note: none: observability hooks weaken the boundary

statement: In a purecap kernel an attacker in a driver can use only capabilities directly or transitively reachable, but ioctl code can reach the calling process's credentials via curthread and escalate to root; kernel-internal APIs were never designed against an in-kernel attacker.
assumptions: Motivates moving the driver to user space
map_note: G-CF: the OS reading or writing compartment state by reachable kernel data

statement: A user-space GPU driver must not control the GPU page tables; GTT management is an OS-vendor-vetted kernel component; only two functions create page-table entries and only for frames backing GPU buffers, so arbitrary main memory cannot be mapped; the GTT component is not callable from user space.
assumptions: Independent of any IOMMU, which may be absent or hypervisor-owned
map_note: G-CF6: the accelerator's translation structure is trusted-component-owned

statement: eBPF interrupt-handler sandboxes are bounded by CHERI to the device's MMIO interface; maps and helper functions are unsupported; GTT-related handlers run natively in the vetted component.
assumptions: Hardened uBPF interpreter
map_note: G-CF6: untrusted interrupt code confined to device registers

statement: MMIO registers are split into safe and unsafe; the driver receives a capability covering most of the MMIO space but excluding the GTT page-table base registers; unsafe-but-needed registers are reached via the privileged component.
assumptions: Mali register map undocumented; indirect apertures unknown
map_note: G-CF6: byte-granular MMIO delegation

statement: Co-located processes spawn with capabilities only to their own memory regions and share only by sending capabilities over Unix domain sockets, permitted only when sender and receiver are in the same address space.
assumptions: Standard sockets invalidate tags
map_note: G-CF: process-granularity compartments in one address space

statement: The co-located-process branch lacks temporal safety; a capability shared then freed must be revoked, and one co-located process must be prevented from munmap-ing a buffer shared with another; posited as small revoker changes but unmeasured.
assumptions: Baseline lacked the temporal-safety subsystem
map_note: GAP-9: shared-buffer lifetime across distrusting principals

statement: Co-located processes have no protection from speculative control-flow attacks because the microarchitecture is unaware of the in-address-space boundary; SPCBEL0 speculation bounds are proposed but cannot be added to Morello silicon.
assumptions: Simulated with ISB
map_note: none: side channels are outside AIVHAI's formal boundary

statement: The GPU is capability-unaware and clears tags when writing to memory.
assumptions: Morello Mali G76
map_note: G-CF6: DMA writes cannot inject capabilities

statement: Threat model: a non-malicious application with a flawed implementation; the adversary can invoke arbitrary malloc/free sequences and arbitrary loads and stores within allocations; the kernel, allocator and runtime are trusted.
assumptions: CHERI-MIPS FPGA prototype
map_note: GAP-9: heap reuse adversary

statement: Cornucopia guarantee: allocators do not reallocate a region until all capabilities to it have been revoked; accesses to a freed object succeed and see the preserved object until revocation, then trap; heap aliasing (use-after-reallocation) is prevented.
assumptions: Allocator enforces spatial safety, hardens free(), and zeroes before reallocation
map_note: GAP-9: reuse gated on global revocation

statement: Non-goals: stack temporal safety; integers derived from capabilities (addresses) are not tracked, and revoked capabilities retain their addresses, so integer confusion is possible; address-space reuse across munmap is not implemented.
assumptions: Later Reloaded adds reservation quarantine for munmap
map_note: GAP-9: identifiers other than capabilities

statement: Complete revocation must reach beyond user memory: all thread register files are swept and the kernel's hoards of user pointers (kqueue cookies, aio) are revoked or cancelled; threads are held at the system-call boundary so ephemeral capabilities reside in trap frames.
assumptions: Kernel memory is not scanned
map_note: GAP-9: the OS is a holder of compartment capabilities

statement: VMMAP-bearing capabilities (allocator-internal, from mmap) are not subject to revocation; malloc strips VMMAP before return; the kernel requires VMMAP on capabilities authorising mapping changes.
assumptions: Revocation distinguishes only TCB from non-TCB
map_note: GAP-4: the only two-level authority distinction revocation supports

statement: Unmediated writes to the shadow bitmap can break temporal safety (a spurious clear lets capabilities to quarantined memory survive); access to a region of the shadow is granted only on presenting a VMMAP capability to the corresponding memory, so distrusting allocators cannot touch each other's shadows.
assumptions: Implemented in integrations, bypassed in the shim experiments
map_note: GAP-4: revocation control is itself a delegated authority

statement: Hierarchical revocation (selectively undoing delegations outside the TCB) is not provided; new architectural mechanisms would be required.
assumptions: Only global revocation of freed heap
map_note: GAP-4 and GAP-9: no per-delegation revocation

statement: Central revocation-epoch guarantee: all capabilities to memory marked quarantined prior to an epoch's start are expunged as of the epoch's end; memory freed during a concurrent scan must wait for the next epoch.
assumptions: Allocators read enqueue/dequeue epoch counters with fences
map_note: GAP-9: the precise reuse precondition

statement: Reloaded invariant: any pointer held in a user thread's register file did not point into quarantine as of the beginning of the last revocation, and any pointer loaded by the application is to an allocation live as of that epoch's start; established by a short stop-the-world register and kernel-hoard scan plus capability load generation traps.
assumptions: Known defects on aliased (copy-on-write) pages not exercised by benchmarks
map_note: GAP-9: reuse precondition on Morello and CHERI-RISC-V

statement: The UAF/UAR gap is tolerated: a pointer to quarantined memory may be dereferenced until a subsequent revocation completes, but never after; within an epoch pointers to memory freed in that epoch are undefined-behaviour accesses.
assumptions: CHERIoT closes this gap
map_note: GAP-9: destruction is not immediate

statement: Revocation tests the capability base, not address; the CHERI ISA ensures bases cannot be taken out of bounds without rendering the capability useless, a property formally verified for Morello.
assumptions: Proof is of the Morello ISA model (Bauereiss et al.), cited by the revocation paper
map_note: GAP-9: the ISA fact the revoker's soundness rests on
correction: Codex review of PR #246, Cycle 1: FilardoGutsteinWoodruffEtAl-24 fn9 attributes the fact to the Morello proof.

statement: Unmapped memory: mmap reservations backed by guard mappings after partial munmap; fully unmapped reservations are quarantined and swept before being freed; implemented but not evaluated.
assumptions: Closes the munmap gap of Cornucopia
map_note: GAP-9: address-space reuse

statement: CHERIvoke guarantee: an allocated object can be accessed only through references derived from the latest allocation of that memory; use-after-reallocation is prevented, strict use-after-free is not.
assumptions: Modelled on x86, sweeps measured on CHERI-MIPS FPGA over dumps
map_note: GAP-9: the original reuse guarantee

statement: Pointers cannot be hidden from the revoker: all memory accesses require a capability, tags identify every capability, and bounds attribute each heap capability to exactly one allocation; revocation is therefore non-probabilistic even against adversarial programs.
assumptions: Allocator sets exact bounds; no 'fuse' of adjacent objects
map_note: GAP-9: completeness of sweeping

statement: CHERIvoke does not address uninitialised data or information leakage between prior and current allocations, and does not address the compartmentalisation threat model in which the local programmer is malicious and shared memory could be improperly freed by either compartment.
assumptions: Heap only; stack excluded
map_note: GAP-4 and GAP-9: distrusting co-owners of a buffer

statement: The allocator is in the TCB; it must hold references to quarantined memory using whole-heap-spanning capabilities whose bases are never quarantined.
assumptions: Definition of temporal safety derives from allocator state
map_note: GAP-9: allocator exemption from revocation

statement: Each CheriRTOS task is confined within a PCC/DDC pair (code section; data and stack); any access outside the domain requires receiving additional capabilities and naming them explicitly.
assumptions: CHERI-64, 32-bit flat address space, no MMU
map_note: G-CF: task isolation by initial capability pair

statement: Fast CCall: entering a domain requires a type-matched sealed PCC/DDC pair; sealed capabilities are immutable and non-dereferenceable so they expose no memory, and the PCC pointer field is the only valid entry point, enforcing CFI between domains.
assumptions: CCallFast bypasses the kernel exception path
map_note: G-CF4: entry only at the sealed entry point

statement: Distributed trusted stacks: a kernel-only register ($KR1C) points to a per-task trusted stack; a kernel CCall helper pushes the caller's PCC/DDC and pops them on return, so the caller's return information cannot be tampered with or cleared and it is always possible to return securely regardless of the callee.
assumptions: Trusted stack depth limited to 4 for determinism
map_note: G-CF4: guaranteed return to caller

statement: Real-time return guarantee: a caller may attach a timeout to a CCall; the timer interrupt checks time stamps on the trusted stack and forces the callee to return on expiry; only trusted tasks may specify timeouts because the timer enables side-channel attacks.
assumptions: Randomised vs full trusted-stack traversal trade-off
map_note: GAP-1: a forced-termination mechanism that AIVHAI defers

statement: Register safety: a caller backs up callee-saved registers and clears all non-argument registers before a CCall; a callee that distrusts the caller clears all registers except return values; the cost is paid only when interacting with untrusted modules.
assumptions: Optional per trust relationship
map_note: G-CF4: register scrub as a caller/callee discipline rather than a TCB action

statement: Secure peripherals: a memory-mapped device is a task holding a capability to its MMIO region; another task may use it only if it holds the sealed pair to CCall into the device task.
assumptions: MMIO delegation only; DMA not addressed
map_note: G-CF6: peripheral access as delegated capability (MMIO, not DMA)

statement: Heap integrity: the header of an in-use chunk holds a capability sealed with the allocator's unique otype carrying the bucket ID; a task cannot forge it, so the allocator verifies that a chunk being freed was allocated by it, preventing freeing arbitrary memory or double-free contamination of free lists.
assumptions: Each task has a unique otype; no temporal safety (per CHERIoT Table 4)
map_note: GAP-9: free-path integrity without revocation

statement: Context switches save and restore the capability register file including PCC and DDC, so a context switch is a domain switch and there is no inherent limit on simultaneous tasks or protection regions.
assumptions: 22 extra cycles per switch
map_note: GAP-1: preemption with per-task capability context

statement: Compartmentalization rests on three underpinnings: a TCB able to protect its own integrity, compartment isolation implemented by the TCB, and controlled communication via call gates to well-defined entry points.
assumptions: Threat model: attacker gains total control of a compromised compartment; supply-chain trojans included
map_note: G-CF: the conceptual decomposition AIVHAI's goal instantiates

statement: Compartment reuse leaks: sensitive data (a key, a parsed URL) not scrubbed before leaving a sandbox is available to the next request; zeroing defends against accidental leakage but not a compromised sandbox, whereas ephemeral sandboxes give more security at creation cost.
assumptions: SOAAP static warning
map_note: GAP-9: reuse across callers without destruction

statement: Lazy initialisation is an anti-pattern for compartmentalisation: libc caching (getservbyname, timegm) or lazily dlopen-ed translation libraries succeed or fail depending on whether initialisation ran before sandbox entry.
assumptions: Found by ktrace and static analysis
map_note: none: functional-correctness hazard of static authority closure

statement: Data replicated between compartments can fall out of sync (gzip compression level not propagated; l_flag read after fork), a distributed-systems correctness hazard of compartmentalisation.
assumptions: Process-based sandboxes
map_note: none

statement: Silent security regression: a pkgsrc patch disabled OpenSSH privilege separation on all platforms except Interix for nine years; the OpenSSH TCB share grew from 31% to 41% of code over 13 years.
assumptions: SOAAP longitudinal analysis
map_note: none: maintenance risk to any compartment policy

statement: The set of memory locations accessible to executing code is the transitive closure of capabilities in its register file and those reachable through them; any capability held during userspace execution descends from those granted to the supervisor at boot and later delegated to userspace.
assumptions: Tagged memory, guarded manipulation
source: WatsonWoodruffNeumannEtAl-15.md L269; WatsonNortonWoodruffEtAl-16.md L106; WatsonNeumannMoore-18.md L146
map_note: A-5: all post-boot authority is a refinement of boot authority

statement: Sealed capabilities are entirely immutable and may not be used to load, store or execute; sealed code and data capabilities are linked by a 24-bit object type that must match for invocation; the ISA never automatically unseals, avoiding unintended amplification.
assumptions: CUnseal requires a capability authorising the type
map_note: G-CF4 and GAP-4: encapsulated references without authority gain

statement: CCall and CReturn as described by the ISA are not sufficient in isolation to implement secure domain transition: the software runtime must ensure that memory allocation and capability distribution implement the required isolation, and that general-purpose and capability register files are flushed of private data and rights before invocation and after return.
assumptions: Hybrid hardware/software transition
map_note: G-CF4: the boundary invariants are a software obligation

statement: Global/local capability flow control: local capabilities may be stored only via Permit_Store_Local capabilities; CheriBSD makes stack capabilities local and heap capabilities non-store-local, and CCall blocks delegation of local capabilities, so memory arguments to invocation must be heap allocated and stack memory cannot be passed by reference; the mechanism restricts the flow of capabilities, not data.
assumptions: Intended to expose delegable memory to revocation and GC policies
map_note: GAP-4: bounded delegation for the duration of an invocation

statement: CCall exception handler: rejects local argument capabilities and a full trusted stack, pushes the caller's $pcc and $idc, installs unsealed callee code and data capabilities, and clears all non-argument general-purpose and capability registers in the TCB so both sides can rely on it.
assumptions: Pseudocode in Figure 6; hardware validates sealing, types, permissions
map_note: G-CF4: entry invariants enforced by the TCB

statement: CReturn exception handler: rejects local return capabilities and an empty trusted stack, pops $idc and $pcc, and clears all non-return-value registers.
assumptions: Pseudocode in Figure 7
map_note: G-CF4: return invariants enforced by the TCB

statement: The compiler's CHERI_CCall calling convention clears unused argument registers in the caller and unused return registers in the callee, since only the compiler knows the function type; CCall/CReturn clear all other registers.
assumptions: Hardware CClearRegs zeroes up to 16 registers with a commit-safe zero mask
source: WatsonWoodruffNeumannEtAl-15.md L138, L439; WatsonNortonWoodruffEtAl-16.md L152, L162, L170
map_note: G-CF4: registers scrubbed

statement: The kernel rejects system calls unless the executing code capability carries the software-defined PERM_SYSCALL/User_Syscall permission; libcheri prohibits system calls within compartments, which must instead invoke system objects (e.g. cheri_fd with the descriptor number embedded in the sealed data capability).
assumptions: Eliminates the kernel syscall interface from the compartment attack surface
source: WatsonWoodruffNeumannEtAl-15.md L391, L404, L457; WatsonNortonWoodruffEtAl-16.md L232, L258
map_note: G-CF: compartments cannot reach the OS except through delegated objects

statement: Signal handlers receive capability registers via an extended frame and execute in an ambient context on a signal stack rather than on a stack borrowed from an untrustworthy object; the runtime may unwind the trusted stack or terminate the object.
assumptions: CHERI faults mapped to SIGPROT
map_note: G-CF4: trap path leaves the compartment's stack

statement: CHERI spatial protection does not natively prevent use-after-free; within one domain rapid reuse is not a vulnerability, but memory passed between domains could lead to temporal vulnerability; the design relies on address-space non-reuse, information flow control and garbage collection, and 'leaked capabilities' are a key concern.
assumptions: Revocation hard by design (no indirection tables)
map_note: GAP-4 and GAP-9: delegation without revocation

statement: Temporal and work-bounded compartmentalisation patterns: sandboxes reset after a packet count or time window limit the window of a successful attacker; an alarm() times out packet processing against infinite loops.
assumptions: tcpdump case study; two CVEs unmitigated as policy issues
map_note: GAP-1 and GAP-9: bounded work and periodic destruction as mitigations

statement: Limitations: the approach depends on the hardware substrate for strong isolation despite the literature on processor side channels, and on C-language TCBs (compiler, allocators, object-file parsing, GC); mitigated by formal modelling of the ISA and software TCBs and minimising the isolation footprint.
assumptions: 2015 status; formal analyses 'being conducted'
map_note: G-CF: residual trust in toolchain and runtime

statement: A hypothetical single-cycle hardware domain crossing (M-Machine style) would sacrifice the trusted intermediary, losing the trusted stack and call-return semantics, TCB-performed register clearing, and system-wide capability-flow guarantees.
assumptions: Would save 145 cycles (18%)
map_note: G-CF4: why the boundary invariants need a trusted intermediary

statement: Architectural properties: provenance validation (only capabilities derived via valid transformations can be used), capability integrity (no in-memory manipulation of encodings), monotonicity (no increase of permissions or bounds); together unforgeability.
assumptions: Stated for CHERI-MIPS; proved elsewhere for ISA models
map_note: G-CF: hardware basis

statement: Abstract capability: every legitimate memory access is via a deliberately constructed abstract capability built by a legitimate provenance chain from primordial capabilities, whole-system across process creation, swapping, syscalls, linking, signals and debugging; the kernel maintains the virtual-to-physical invariants that make the architectural capability realise it.
assumptions: 'Purely conceptual model'; formalisation is future work
map_note: G-CF: the OS-level counterpart of the compartment authority graph

statement: Kernel startup narrows boot capabilities to ones separately covering userspace, kernel code and kernel data; each process receives a fresh principal with a disjoint root, physical memory disjoint from other processes except deliberately shared mappings.
assumptions: Kernel in the TCB; relies on the low-address user map being correct
map_note: A-5: root authority is refined before any untrusted code runs

statement: The kernel accesses user memory only through the user-provided capability (not its own elevated authority); non-capability copyin/copyout return errors for CheriABI processes; tags are stripped on user-kernel copies except through special interfaces; management interfaces expose virtual addresses, not kernel capabilities.
assumptions: Prevents confused-deputy attacks via the kernel; ioctl/sysctl cases partially translated
map_note: G-CF: the OS does not read or write beyond what the compartment delegated

statement: DDC is set to NULL in CheriABI, eliminating legacy integer-pointer loads and stores; all accesses are intentional through explicit capabilities with reduced permissions and narrowed bounds; PCC is bounded to the shared object.
assumptions: Code bounds are per shared object, not minimal
map_note: G-CF4: no DDC, bounded PCC in userspace

statement: Swapping, signal delivery and debugging preserve the abstract capability: tags are recorded and capabilities rederived on swap-in from an appropriate root; debugger-injected capabilities are derived from the target's own roots and never propagated between principals.
assumptions: Break in the architectural chain bridged by the kernel
map_note: A-5: re-derivation from roots is a kernel privilege

statement: malloc returns capabilities bounded to the request, non-executable, with VMMAP stripped so they cannot remap memory under the allocator; mmap/shmat return bounded capabilities and munmap/shmdt require VMMAP, preventing replacement of arbitrary memory without a valid capability.
assumptions: sbrk unsupported
map_note: GAP-9: mapping lifetime guarded by a software permission

statement: Intra-object memory-safety violations are not protected (12 of 291 BOdiagsuite tests) and cannot be without compatibility impact; sub-object bounds are future work.
assumptions: container_of patterns
map_note: none: within-allocation confusion inside a compartment

statement: Capabilities act on virtual memory via CPU instructions only; DMA devices and IOMMUs also interact with memory, and attacks via IOMMUs show the need for protection beyond the CPU (future work).
assumptions: Cites Thunderclap
map_note: G-CF6: the gap the DMA position paper addresses

statement: The hybrid kernel leaves most kernel pointers unprotected; a pure-capability kernel would increase protection.
assumptions: 2019 status; 2024 article reports a referentially and spatially safe kernel
map_note: G-CF: OS-side integrity

statement: Threat model: well-intentioned native C code may contain memory-safety vulnerabilities enabling arbitrary code with the native code's permissions; the JVM is assumed trustworthy (asymmetric distrust); sandboxed native code must be unable to violate any Java memory-safety guarantee and must be constrained by the SecurityManager for OS resources.
assumptions: JamVM on CHERI-MIPS FPGA
map_note: G-CF: a host runtime is the OS analogue

statement: Object pointers, method IDs and field IDs passed to native code are sealed with distinct keys; hardware prevents modification and the JVM cheaply checks type on return, preventing the write-anywhere type confusion possible with table-less SFI sandboxes.
assumptions: C strings from native code also validated
map_note: GAP-4: opaque delegated references

statement: Buffer capabilities handed to native code have load-capability and store-capability permissions removed so native code cannot store pointers in them that it or another sandbox could later retrieve; read-only direct buffers also lose store permission.
assumptions: Arrays of Java objects accessed only by copy
map_note: G-CF4: data-only I/O buffers, the exact mechanism the CF draft proposes

statement: Sandboxed code cannot issue system calls; each is proxied through libcheri with default ENOSYS and selective SecurityManager checks; arbitrary mmap can escape the sandbox; interposition must copy pathname arguments to non-shared memory before validation to avoid races under concurrent sharing.
assumptions: ioctl entirely prevented
map_note: G-CF and GAP-1: service proxying under concurrent delegated memory

statement: Asymmetric distrust implemented by a second trampoline and a kernel trap-handler change that skips capability-flow checks when the object type has its high bit set; only system objects allocated by trusted code receive such types.
assumptions: Native code may pass stack pointers to the JVM but not the converse
map_note: GAP-4: a controlled relaxation of flow checks

statement: Revocation of delegated references: a background thread scans each non-executing sandbox's touched pages, identifies every capability by tag, and overwrites released object references and buffer capabilities with NULL (sealed case via hash table; unsealed subset case via a red-black tree of delegated arrays); direct buffers are pinned until a scan finds no capability to them.
assumptions: Sandbox memory 16 MB; synchronous variant in first prototype
map_note: GAP-9: per-sandbox revocation of delegated references

statement: On a fault or invalid JNI argument the JVM unwinds the trusted stack, raises a Java exception, and resets the sandbox because its state is assumed undefined; method-scoped sandboxes are created and destroyed per invocation.
assumptions: Sandbox creation is 216K instructions
map_note: GAP-9: reset-on-fault and per-call destruction

statement: Sandbox setup grants native code its entire heap via DDC, so fine-grained memory safety within the sandbox is advisory; 56 of 59 security-critical JDK native bugs would have been defended; TOCTOU file races would not.
assumptions: Tan and Croft study
map_note: G-CF: containment of a memory-unsafe compartment

statement: DMA threat model: CPU, cache hierarchy and DRAM are trustworthy; some privileged software is trustworthy; peripherals are autonomous with their own firmware and may be attached by an attacker or compromised; two classes: untrustworthy hardware and software, or trustworthy hardware with untrustworthy software.
assumptions: Rowhammer, Infiniband, USB message protocols out of scope
map_note: G-CF6: the adversary a capability-aware NPU shim must withstand

statement: For a capability microcontroller with DMA, unless the device holds appropriate authority: devices cannot access memory outside permitted regions, cannot forge new capabilities, cannot expand the rights of existing capabilities, and must preserve intentionality so valid capabilities are not used for incorrect purposes.
assumptions: Position paper; no implementation
map_note: G-CF6: the four DMA containment properties

statement: Tag clearing baseline: devices store only data; any DMA write to a capability in memory clears its tag; the I/O interconnect carries no tags and cannot reach tag storage; ideally I/O writes also invalidate cached capabilities; this preserves capability integrity but not the integrity of data pointed to, so device accesses still need constraint.
assumptions: Devices use integer addresses
map_note: G-CF6: necessary but insufficient

statement: MPU-for-DMA and Capability Search Unit: device requests are checked against 8-16 ranges or capabilities; the CSU is configured atomically by writing a capability, so software cannot populate it with authority it does not hold, and the table may be delegated to the application; both lack scalability.
assumptions: Parallel lookups cost area and power
map_note: G-CF6: IOPMP-class mechanism with capability intentionality

statement: IOMMU protection is page-granular, page-walks are expensive, and IOTLB revocation is asynchronous, opening a temporal vulnerability; in practice IOMMUs are poorly used for performance reasons.
assumptions: Cites Thunderclap and IOMMU performance literature
map_note: G-CF6: limits of the IOMMU option

statement: ALUT/CLUT: a one-level index-plus-offset translation with bounds (O < Omax) and permissions per entry; a CLUT holds capabilities, so mappings cannot be constructed without software holding valid capabilities, rights transfer correctly from software to hardware without privileged management; revocation is a null write that synchronises the last-level cache.
assumptions: Virtually-addressed CLUT needs an ASID and IOMMU for translation
map_note: G-CF6: a capability-mediated DMA shim design

statement: Devices with trustworthy hardware may consume capability descriptor rings and run CHERI internally, but a separate capability root must exist within the device and tags must not pass over the interconnect in either direction; an IOMMU, CSU or CLUT is still required to constrain the device's requests; shared memory needs segregation or colouring.
assumptions: Defence in depth; the device's initial capability set bounds its firmware
map_note: G-CF6: the Coral NPU front-end case, RISC-V firmware under a separate root

statement: The CHERI C memory object model is mechanised in Coq (extracted into Cerberus) and intended as a basis for later mechanised proofs of properties such as provenance validity and capability integrity; no such proofs are reported.
assumptions: Morello chosen for implementation-defined aspects via Sail-extracted Coq; 94-test suite validates against Clang and GCC
source: ZalivaMemarianAlmeidaEtAl-24.md L46, L90, L432-436, L508, L640
map_note: none: language-level semantics, no compartment property

statement: Runtime capability checks cannot subsume compile-time provenance checks: without a revocation mechanism provenance is temporally unique while capabilities are not, so a pointer to a killed heap object and one to a new object at the same address can coexist; the redundancy of the bounds check under capabilities is believed but not formally proved.
assumptions: PNVI-ae-udi provenance semantics
map_note: GAP-9: reuse without revocation breaks provenance-based reasoning

statement: PNVI-ae-udi: provenance is tracked in the abstract machine, not via integers; integer-to-pointer casts recreate provenance only for exposed live objects; CHERI C with capabilities for all pointers is a stricter model than the proposed provenance semantics.
assumptions: Executable Cerberus semantics; empirical FreeBSD corpus study
map_note: none: provenance vocabulary only

statement: Formal modelling of the Morello and CHERI-MIPS ISAs supported machine-checked proof that the ISAs enforce correctness of capability bounds comparison and isolation of arbitrary code by compartmentalization mechanisms.
assumptions: Proof is over the ISA model (Sail to Isabelle), for arbitrary code constrained by capabilities; no software switcher is modelled
source: WatsonChisnallClarkeEtAl-24.md L270-272, ref 12 L389; WatsonNeumannMoore-18.md L299
map_note: G-CF: the only mechanized compartment-isolation result in the corpus

statement: Penetration testing by MSRC on WebKit JSC and a DARPA crowd-sourced exercise identified two software-TCB vulnerabilities and led to sealing all control-flow pointers; MSRC reported over two-thirds deterministic mitigation of memory-safety vulnerabilities.
assumptions: Prototype implementation
map_note: G-CF4: sealed control-flow pointers as an entry invariant

statement: Quarantine-and-sweep temporal safety is not applicable to stack allocations because of their frequency, and no obvious compiler technique complements CHERI for use-after-scope; uninitialized values are omitted from CHERI's properties and rely on zeroing.
assumptions: MSRC analysis assumes initialisation mitigations continue
map_note: GAP-9: stack and uninitialised-value gaps

statement: Compartmentalization strengthens the adversary model from 'imperfect programmer' to 'malicious programmer' and is listed as future work beyond memory safety.
assumptions: 2024 status
map_note: G-CF: the AIVHAI adversary is the one CHERI's authors call future work

statement: Software fault isolation and compartmentalization allow continued operation through privilege minimization despite effective exploitation of memory unsafety, constraining attacks that have already achieved arbitrary code execution; strong memory safety should eventually be grounded in formally verified designs whose TCBs are vulnerability-free.
assumptions: Standardisation position; timeline to 2047
map_note: G-CF: the category AIVHAI's claim belongs to

statement: Complete mediation: CHERI capabilities are unforgeable and the mechanism nonbypassable; any attempt to modify a capability yields something that is no longer a capability; fail-safe defaults: no Hydra-like amplification, strict monotonicity of privileges.
assumptions: Principle-level restatement
map_note: G-CF and GAP-4: no amplification during delegation

statement: Least common mechanism: covert channels are not considered in the CHERI ISA and must be dealt with in implementation.
assumptions: Shared-resource exhaustion and clock channels named
map_note: none: outside AIVHAI's formal boundary by policy

statement: Intentional use: when multiple rights are available, the selection used to authorise work must be explicit, countering confused-deputy problems; applied throughout CHERI including explicit capability registers for load/store and the sealed object-capability model.
assumptions: Twelfth principle added at Watson's suggestion

statement: At reset full capabilities are granted to the boot environment, then delegated and refined from firmware to OS kernel, from kernel to userspace, and within user compartments.
